#4151. Atmosfar is a giddy aerial exploration game after the heart of No Man's Sky, but I'm already trying to escape it

Oh hi there! Why yes, I am free to chat. Please excuse the wind noise, I'm currently tumbling to my doom in Atmosfar, after getting lost in a cloud bank and exhausting my fuel. This kind of thing happens to me regularly in Atmosfar - an open world survival game that plays out across clusters of floating islands, with players scooting about in adorable, propellor-powered airships.

Many of the islands are quite large, with proper landing pads and bases set up by NPC scavengers. Many of them teem with non-human life: rainforests full of nectar droplets and carnivorous plants, meadows of ponderous honking lizards, and mossy grottos where you'll find caches of batteries and possibly get eaten by mantids. It's important to make the most of these larger islands, gathering materials for crafting at your deployable campsite (which straps pleasingly to the back of your whirring fly-mobile). It's particularly important to mine hydrogen crystals you can refine into fuel.

None of that's for me, though! I am a true spirit of the sky. The only fuel I need is my imagination. The only objective marker I acknowledge is the omnidirectional Call to Adventure. Besides, when you do run out of fuel in Atmosfar, you're actually unlocking two exciting minigames. The first consists of leaping from the cockpit and vainly trying to jetpack to the nearest walkable surface. The second consists of racing to overtake your plummeting airship and re-enter the cockpit before you smash into any islands beneath. I'm playing that second minigame right now. Come to papa, my beautiful turboprop son! Ah, balls.

Atmosfar is out in Steam early access today, with plans to stay in early access for at least nine months. I think it has some juice, though I am admittedly already trying to play it against the grain - and at times, trying to do things its technology doesn't quite allow.

It casts you as an interplanetary pioneer who, due to some minor infraction, has been locked up in a factory: a dreary opening area with some corpo-satire elements, from which you are soon liberated by an electrical storm. Busting past the sentry drones, you scramble down a cliffside and discover your very first Wasp hovercar. From there, you have more or less free rein of the game's opening biome, though there's a critical path of tutorials and NPC encounters you'll want to follow for the sake of unlocks, like the jetpack.

The scattered islands do a fair job of luring you from your HUD objectives (the HUD itself is a bit murky, in any case – I struggled to make connections between waypoints and quests in my journal). Even if there's nothing to capital-i Interact with, it's a pleasure to alight on some drifting gobbet of soil and flowers, peer into the crevices, and maybe take a few photos of distant astral mountains.

The searing emptiness all around makes the design of each island feel more precise and careful, gift-wrapped for the player. I find that I'm most interested in the tinier islands, the ones that were presumably a secondary consideration for developers Apog Labs, and maybe handed off to a junior staffer. I gaze at a random grass tuft and try to guess how much ingenuity went into the placement of something many pilots will totally ignore.

I'm already chafing against the survival systems a bit, however. Based on a couple of hours of cloudsteading, Atmosfar's core ingredients aren't particularly novel or involving. There's no tree-chopping, thank god, but you will spend many moments pointing your extractor at a nugget of glowing resourcegook, splitting it into plastic sheets and steel girders and so forth.

Many of the opening missions involve toing and froing between deposits and your airship or camp. It's humdrum stuff. The game's non-player scavengers seem like quest-givers first, characters second. Your inventory size is limited, to begin with. Deeper in, there's the opportunity to construct a huge airbase, the Cloud Cruiser, which I'm really hoping doesn't need refuelling. Although it would be a great joke to accidentally drop one with several co-op buds inside.

I've spent most of my two hours in Atmosfar in headlong retreat from the tutorial quests, trying to reach places I sense I'm not supposed to, without paying my dues to the crafting system. This includes both the ruddier, volcanic areas higher up, which I do believe I can reach, if I bother to refine enough fuel. But I'm more captivated, right now, by what lies beneath.

During a nighttime mission to gather eggs for some outpost chef, I gave into curiosity and aimed my Wasp straight down, spiralling past lonely stalactites with no creature population, into a swirling turquoise abyss full of bare, indistinct rock. As I descended, the game's tech began to creak and fizzle, as though strained by increasing gravity. My ride's exhaust condensed and flattened into glitchy flakes.

I ignored the simulation's protests, holding my course like Ahab aiming a harpoon at Moby Dick's kisser, till a "leaving mission area" reset timer yanked me up short. I ascended to just above the cut-off point, and gawped at the horizon. A juddering white ring enclosed the world, surrounded by wrinkled LIDAR pulses that made me think of thoughts coursing through brain tissue.

Now, this was an adventure. I flapped around a bit, battling turbulence, and managed to land on one of the weirdly unadorned, formless boulders. Who made this? Some procedural generation system, or did somebody actually have to 'hand-craft' these places that are probably not for serious human inquiry or habitation? I shot a few flares over the side and tried to deploy my campsite, but there was too little space on the boulder. Then the sun rose, slowly staining the milky blue fastness pink, and revealing the crisper silhouettes of the properly designed and navigable islands high above.

That last screenshot is my favourite so far - the rosy, rugged beauty of Atmosfar and the bizarre quirks of its technology reaching a strangely persuasive accord. There's only one issue: I've run out of fuel again. I guess I could yeet myself into the void and reset to the nearest landing pad, but that doesn't feel like something a true Spirit of the Sky would do. I guess I'll have to enlist another RPS scribe as a co-op partner and have them come fetch me. Perhaps they can complete the tutorials first and rock up in one of those Cloud Cruiser things. In the meantime, you can get your fill of Atmosfaring via Steam.

#4150. Don't worry, GTA 6's cars can drive for ages before their fuel tanks need refilling, leaving me wondering why this motor management's been added at all

Right, before you groan too hard, I promise that after I write this I'll take a break of indeterminate length from writing articles which amount to wondering aloud why a thing that's in GTA 6 is in GTA 6. Cars which need refuelling. It's not an addition there'd not been any hint was coming before today, as with the smell reaction system, leaks having hinted at fuel management all the way back in August.

Since that point, it's been confirmed as in the version of the game Rockstar will be shipping to consoles (boo) next month and PC at some point after that. Edge's GTA 6 long read notes the existence of fuel gauges and engine health readouts, but it also caveats them in what seems an insistence from Rockstar that the first of these features isn't designed to make filling up something the player necessarily has to do often or spend much time on when they do.

GTA 6's cars, according to Edge, can drive vast distances before they reach the point of running low on fuel, while refuelling is something you can do in quick and fuss-free fashion. On one hand, having cars that can barely drive three streets without sputtering to a halt and making the gas station experience a clunky chore that takes ages clearly would've both been terrible moves.

However, the fact the system's lenience is being emphasised has me wondering why it was worth adding at all. To be fair, Edge do outline that the variable amounts of gas in tanks does work with other new mechanics to add more unpredictability to crime sprees and rewards taking a bit more time to prepare a battle plan for robberies. If there's a chance that random ride you'd usually nick from an NPC on running out into the street with your loot might be running on fumes that won't get you through the ensuing police chase, that makes having proper getaway arrangements made prior to the stick-up more important. Then again, it seems any weapons your character's not got room to carry at any time are stored in their car's trunk in GTA 6 - rather than just shoved in pockets that can somehow fit an RPG - so always bringing your own wheels along on a job might be a no-brainer regardless.

All that in mind, this fuel management feels to me like it might suffer a fate similar to vampire RPG The Blood of Dawnwalker's time mechanics. If you've not played Dawnwalker - you should, here's my review - its devs Rebel Wolves based their story around giving the player 30 days and nights in which to find a way to save their family, lest mysterious consequences occur. Cue some folks feeling put off by the idea their adventuring would be restricted by any sort of time constraints, others concluding that the timer was too lenient to fulfil its role of focusing them on getting their task done in suitably rapid fashion, and people like me feeling like they had about the right amount of days left by the time they were in position to launch one of the game's final missions.

Managing fuel in games, especially ones in which people are used to being able to just get in a car and drive for as long as they fancy, tends to be similarly polarising. I can see some GTA 6 players raging against the idea that they've ever got to stop rampaging or partying to do something as mundane as fill up. I can see others being disappointed that, in trying to ensure that first group aren't put off, Rockstar have diluted the mechanic to the point it's not forcing players to fill up at a cadence that feels realistic in the way features like this are supposed to at their best. Many may end up thinking an ideal compromise has been reached. This can be the case with any feature in any game to a degree and all of us should at least try a game in the form its devs envisioned before resorting to moaning for more options or seeking out mods.

Though, as the driving games out there already prove, when it comes to fuel simulation it's usually best for studios to go all-in on committing to the mechanic if they're going to implement it, rather than trying to occupy a mushy middle ground. In full-blown sims like either of SCS's truck sims, SnowRunner, and iRacing, it's an obvious inclusion because the central appeal of those games lies in mirroring motoring in realistic detail. In open-world arcade racers like Forza Horizon, Need For Speed, and Burnout, it's usually cast aside as the sort of thing that'd be more of an annoying limitation than a welcome wrinkle, with filling stations that do appear often limited to dishing out nitrous or boost for extra speed instead.

Up until now, GTA's always fallen on the latter side of the fence and honestly seemed at home there. It's been an action-filled crime romp, not a life sim, and its cars have been designed to best suit that identity. With 6, though, Rockstar are skewing harder into the latter, as they did with Red Dead Redemption 2. RDR2's beloved, the majority of players could well end up adjusting to or appreciating this extra layer of thinking they'll have to do whenever they fire up their wheels. In my estimation, however, fuel management's the biggest risk Rockstar are taking with any of their new additions. The series is called Grand Theft Auto, after all. You're only messing with a wheeled aspect of it so central that they're right there in the name.

If you pick up a DMZ bank vault keycard, you must first power the keycard reader and find a code

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you gain access to any of the MW4 DMZ bank vaults, you can pick up some serious cash alongside other valuable loot. Cash itself, though, is perhaps one of the most valuable resources you can exfil with thanks to DMZ's Vendor, who will sell you weapons and gear before your next mission - but they don't come cheap, making bank heists a worthwhile endeavor.

Pretty much everything you need for a bank heist can be found in or around the bank itself, but it's not entirely obvious what you need to actually do to get the vault open, so if you're looking to crank the vault door open for yourself, here's what you need to know.

There are four bank vaults in the MW4 DMZ map: One north of Songdo Wharf, another to the south of Wolves Stadium, one inside The Grid, and another in Cheongun Village.The three banks not located within The Grid are smaller bank branches and are much easier to loot as The Grid is an extreme-threat area. If you're heisting for the first time, I'd recommend starting with the eastern-most bank branch, to the north of Songdo Wharf.

To open DMZ bank vaults, you need three things: a car battery, a keycard, and a note showing most of the vault's unlock code. With these things in hand, follow these steps to unlock the vault:

Of course you'll be challenged during this process as your enemies will come after you, so take them out as and when they appear, particularly if you're tackling the main bank tower in The Grid. For that one, you'll definitely need to equip the best MW4 guns you've unlocked in the extraction mode, as well as a decent armor vest and at least one medkit.

As I've mentioned above, all of the required items can be found in or around the bank itself if you're lucky. Both the keycard and the code are always located within the bank, but a car battery can only be found in gas station stores, and you're not guaranteed to find one. While there is a gas station right next to the smaller bank branch, you're stuffed if there's no battery. There are three gas stations near the eastern branch, though, so your chances of finding a battery are much higher. You can also exfil with a battery, so look for one whenever you're near a gas station, then you can take it into a new match when you're thinking of robbing a bank.

For the keycard and code, simply look around the bank. The keycard is obvious, and the code is on a piece of paper. You'll only get the first three digits for the code, so you'll have to figure out the fourth via the process of elimination, but it's always the last digit.

#4148. Queen's Domain is a brilliant King's Field-alike RPG that forces you to walk so you can learn to fly

I would also have accepted "Prince's Place" or "Baron's Turf"

FromSoftware's elderly King's Field games aren't really celebrated for their feeling of agility. They are glorious first-person trudgefests, a treacle-thick waltz of swinging and spellcraft, with players wobbling in and out of attack range like British men who aren't sure whether the other man wants a hug. Unlike in the later Dark Souls action-RPGs, to which King's Field owes some of its retrospective popularity, there's no dodge-roll to grease the wheels.

Out this week on Steam, Queen's Domain is often as ponderous as King's Field, but it's also an exercise in steady, triumphant acceleration. Ultimately, it wants you to fly. To this end, it equips you - well, once you've boshed a huge skeleton sentinel - with a fancy windblade that lets you perform an aerial dash, speeding your manouevres while allowing you to reach new areas.

You'll find socketable gems that extend the dash, gradually bringing offshore islands and collapsed castle parapets within reach. I'm around four hours into Queen's Domain, and right now, the overall objective is tricking out that enchanted blade: heading down one leg of a marvellous, knotty world, retrieving a gem, and returning along another path, while keeping an eye out for nooks and platforms that once seemed like cordoned-off backdrop.

While an obvious quick-select default, the windblade doesn't make the 50 or so other weapons in the game obsolete, partly because enemies are distinguished by damage type: skellingtons are tougher against swords, while spears tend to bounce off malformed rodent ladybugs. All the weapons level up with use, and all of them have special abilities: the first spear you acquire has a retreating stab, useful against grasshopper chickens with lunging kicks, while the basic wooden club has a pounce move, skipping the lengthy swinging animation that is the weapon's major disadvantage.

For all these flourishes, combat is often as reassuringly stodgy as I remember King's Field being on the early PlayStation consoles. The pace is set by the need to charge your attacks, holding the button till the wind-up consumes your whole stamina bar; spamming blows is much less efficient.

350 words in, and I haven't mentioned the standout attraction in Queen's Domain – the landscape itself, an absurdly lovely expanse of mossy arches, chopped pillars and racked tombs that evokes Shadow of the Colossus and Vagrant Story as much as it does FromSoftware. It's a beautiful place, a haunting recovery of PS2 aesthetics that runs comfortably on integrated graphics. Or at least, it's beautiful until you start screwing around with focal length and lurid filters in the Photo Mode (see below).

The archipelago's interwoven paths are structured around save crystals where you can rest at the price of respawning enemies, but unlike in Souls, enemies eventually respawn of their own accord, appearing in different combinations as you pass certain milestones.

If this last wrinkle creates more potential for ambush, you can shape encounters using your secondary weapons, beginning with a belt of throwing daggers hanging from a shipwreck. I specify the location because embarrassingly, I managed to overlook them for the first hour – in general, Queen's Domain doesn't highlight collectible objects as flagrantly as certain recent blockbusters.

You get an endless supply of daggers, governed by a cooldown. The best thing about them initially is that you can use them to murder the highly annoying laser eyeballs that deck the tree trunks, often zapping you in the back while you're battling something else. Beyond that, you'll use them to bait individuals away from mobs, luring them towards killzones with plenty of strafing room, or getting them jammed behind monoliths so that you can bop their noggins at leisure.

I've got over 30 hours of Queen's Domain left to burn, according to devs Freshly Baked. Unlike with a lot of the non-review games I've dipped into this year, I feel like I might actually go the distance. More thoughts to follow, possibly! If you're new to King's Fieldalikes, you may find this stifling and frustrating at first. Even if you do know your King's Fields, you'll likely perish a lot. But hopefully, the landscape's magnificence and the increasing swagger of the combat system will get you over the hump. The game launches tomorrow, and there's still a demo on Steam as of writing.

#4147. How To Preload GTA 6 In Full On Xbox Series X|S (Even If You Haven't Bought It)

All 200GB+ goes live in just a few hours' time

The official preload for GTA 6 is literally just a few hours away at the time of writing, and it means everyone will be able to install all 200GB+ of the game on Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S ahead of launch on November 19th.

Here are the official preload / preinstall times for GTA 6 on Xbox Series X|S, as we recently highlighted on Pure Xbox:

News GTA 6 Download Size & Preload Times Officially Revealed For Xbox Series X|S

So, there are two ways to preload GTA 6 on Xbox Series X|S depending on whether you have or haven't bought it yet. If you've pre-ordered the game, payment should have now been taken out of your account, and you'll be able to preload it by going to the Microsoft Store app on your Xbox console and searching for Grand Theft Auto VI.

The page you're looking for is the one in the image at the top of this article, although instead of a "pre-order" button, you should see the ability to install the game if you've bought it already. This will install a 300MB placeholder file until 12am GMT on November 10th, after which time the full 200GB download will become available as an update.

If you run into any issues with this, it's worth doing a restart of your console after the full preload goes live.

"On XBOX Series X|S, pre-loading begins globally on Tuesday, November 10 at 12 a.m. GMT. Code-in-box versions for both consoles should be available from retailers beginning November 12. The pre-load file will require up to 212 GB depending on your device, so make sure you've got ample space to begin pre-loading as soon as possible."

If you haven't bought GTA 6 yet but still want to preload it on Xbox Series X|S, you can do so by opening up the Xbox mobile app, going to the "Store" page (represented by a bag icon) and searching for Grand Theft Auto VI. You're specifically looking for "Grand Theft Auto VI" - not the Bundle version, but the standalone version.

In our case, it showed up as the fourth option down - you should see a variant of the following page when you open it:

Again, hitting the install button prior to 12am GMT on November 10th will install a small placeholder file, and then the full 200GB+ download will become available when the full game preload goes live.

That means everyone (except Xbox One owners, of course) has the ability to download GTA 6 on their Xbox consoles later today, so be sure to clear some room ahead of time - it's going to take up a heck of a lot of storage space!

News Here's Another 30+ New GTA 6 Screenshots To Drool Over

#4146. Switch 2 Supposedly Jailbroken Via Software-Only Exploit

Update: It's apparently been patched in the latest update

Update [Tue 10th Nov 2026, 2am]: Following the Switch 2 firmware update today (Version 23.5.0), it seems this jailbreak has now been patched. As OatmealDome explains on social media:

The OS exploit used in the recent jailbreak has been patched in version 23.5.0.

"Dumping and modding games will be impossible again from this point forward, with the exception of some cartridge games (and maybe game updates) that are released in the near future.

"While game exploits like SmileBASIC and Civilization VII still exist, it is no longer possible to "escape" the game starting with 23.5.0. This effectively means that the capabilities of homebrew are locked to whatever the game can do already (i.e. not much)."

News Nintendo Switch 2 System Update 23.5.0 Is Now Live, Here Are The Full Patch Notes

Adds eShop gifting feature support and more

If we hear any significant developments about this, we'll let you know. You can see the original story below:

Original Story: [Fri 23rd Oct, 2026 03:55 BST]: Nintendo appears to have removed the programming software SmileBASIC 4 from the eShop following the supposed discovery of a Switch 2 jailbreak.

The "software-only" tethered jailbreak 'ns2jb' was apparently created by Sammy 'pepsipu' Hajhamid, with the help of OpenAI's Codex.

It allows arbitrary native code to run, and can supposedly be used to "run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games" as well as back up save files. It uses the Switch 2's latest firmware 23.0.1 and requires access to the now-delisted Switch title.

The security researcher and modder believes this is the "first such exploit for the Switch 2" and claims to have successfully added the characters "cinnamoroll, peter griffin, hatsune miku, and more" into Mario Kart World to demonstrate its capabilities.

"This lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO. To my knowledge, it’s the first such exploit for the Switch 2. To demonstrate the capabilities of this jailbreak, Codex modded a Switch 2 exclusive, Mario Kart World."

As this is a "software-only" exploit, it means the minute the Switch 2 is powered off, you're back at square one.

Although the Switch game SmileBASIC 4 has seemingly vanished, Nintendo hasn't openly acknowledged this exploit. However, the creator behind this jailbreak says they're "excited to see all the upcoming Switch 2 homebrew, emulation, and modding".

This isn't the first time something like this has been discovered, either. SmileBASIC was also used for homebrew exploits during the 3DS generation.

News SmileBASIC Gets Taken Down from the 3DS eShop Due to A Homebrew Exploit

If we hear any significant developments or updates about this latest jailbreak, we'll let you know.

[source theverge.com, via notebookcheck.net]

Late to the party, but I kinda wanted to chime in and say that based on the comments, there is a HUGE misunderstanding about exactly how "big" or useful this exploit is. In an absolute best case scenarios, where this couldn't be patched out and there was unlimited time and resources ... this never leads to kernel access. And this is far from best case; it requires a tethered connection to work and is dependent on easily patchable software vulnerabilities.

It's not NOTHING. It's already been used to gain access to some privileged file systems and it might eventually allow for homebrew on very specific unpatched Switch 2s while (and ONLY WHILE) they are connected to PCs. If you're an enthusiast who is excited by that, power to you! I hope it happens. But for casuals, the best way to look at this news is this: Before it happened, no one had discovered any trace of a viable path to a "hacked" Switch 2. After this discovery ... no one has discovered any trace of a viable path to a "hacked" Switch 2. Nothing has changed on that front.

#4145. The Death Stranding Series Has Been Played By Way More People Than You'd Expect

The two Death Stranding games have been modest sellers since their launches, generating more sales than most AAA titles, but not on the same level as other console-defining experiences.

According to official numbers, the first game sold over five million copies. Sales stats relating to the sequel have never been shared, but analyst estimates suggested 1.4 million units were sold during its first few days on the market. In the years since their releases, these totals will have only gone up.

Now we have a new milestone, though, as revealed by Kojima Productions: the Death Stranding series has been played by over 28 million people.

In a social media post to celebrate the first game's seventh anniversary, Hideo Kojima posted a graphic confirming "28 million Porters worldwide". That is 28 million players, not 28 million sales. The image clarifies the total encompasses all console and PC versions of the two games, and anyone who has played them on a subscription service.

Of course, the first Death Stranding started out as a PS4 exclusive, but then made its way to PC less than a year after launch. A Director's Cut version for PS5 then arrived in September 2021, and then in 2024, the game really expanded its availability: it released on iOS, Amazon Luna, and Xbox Series X|S.

The first game is also available on PS Plus Extra, which will be one of the subscription services helping to boost the player numbers.

As for Death Stranding 2, it's just on PS5 and PC for now.

Two of the defining games for the PS4 and PS5 generations, I awarded a rare 10/10 score to both games upon their releases. For the first game, I said: "Death Stranding doesn’t raise the bar for any particular genre, it creates an entirely new one."

Kojima Productions expanded on that original idea with the sequel: "In what will prove to be one of the defining games of the PS5 generation, Death Stranding 2: On the Beach is a profound achievement of design, gameplay, narrative, and visuals. As all four meet in the middle, Kojima Productions has crafted a cinematic spectacle that flawlessly transitions between action and traversal, all wrapped up in the most absorbing of narratives."

Review Death Stranding - Hideo Kojima's Latest Masterpiece Has Arrived

Review Death Stranding 2 (PS5) - A Masterpiece in Every Sense

Welcome to today's edition of pedantry corner:

As any maths fans will tell you, the conclusion of 28 million people is unwarranted. As that figure combines all sales and streaming it does not allow for the fact that the same person could have played on two or more different formats. It is also a fair assumption that a large proportion of Death Stranding 2 players also played the first game and have therefore been counted twice.

All we can fairly say is that up to 28 million people have played (and it is probably closer to half of that).

Of course any physical copy could be enjoyed by a limitless number of people. So the real number could actually be in the trillions.

#4144. Celeste and TowerFall have been removed from the Xbox store in a move to "support the BDS boycott" against Microsoft

This follows fellow indie dev House House announcing Big Walk will not be coming to Xbox

It's a good day to love Celeste! Earlier today it was discovered that Celeste had been removed from the Xbox Store while it remained on the PlayStation and Nintendo digital storefronts. Now, as shared by the game's co-creator Maddy Thorson, it's been confirmed that both Celeste and TowerFall were removed from store expressly in support of the BDS called boycott against Xbox over Microsoft providing support to the Israeli military as it enacts its genocide of the Palestinian people.

A larger statement hasn't been made by other Celeste developers or Thorson's current studio EXOK Games, but the larger more important point is that the games are no longer available for purchase on the Xbox Store. Earlier this month, House House, developer of one of the biggest indies of the year Big Walk, also shared their own support for the BDS movement and Microsoft boycott announcement by announcing their (quite excellent) social puzzle game will not be launching on Xbox for the foreseeable future. Developer Origame Digital also made an incredibly potent statement denouncing the genocide in their latest game, Penguin's Colony.

For those who’re asking, yes we delisted Celeste and TowerFall on XBox. We did this to support the BDS boycott

For those not in the know, BDS called for the boycott of Microsoft and Xbox games and hardware last year over the tech company providing AI software to the Israeli military which was used specifically to target Palestinian civilians; Microsoft have even confirmed that they were providing this software. They remain on the BDS boycott list due to the fact they continue to provide the Israeli military with other services such as email and file management systems, as well as for "combat and intelligence activities."

The actions of EXOK Games, House House and Origame Digital come at a time of a growing pushback against Xbox over Microsoft's support of the military movement, in part from No Games for Genocide, an organisation made up of developers and industry practitioners (disclaimer: I myself am an organiser at NGFG). These actions show how possible it is to express solidarity with the Palestinian people, and are a good example to follow.

#4143. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel will be an Elder Scrolls game about the infinite mysteries of the Elder Scrolls, report with some plot hintage claims

Also, it's claimed to be set in the place most heavily rumoured since that 2018 teaser

As Xbox's execs continue to pine for game-related announcements to fill in the gaps between their rounds of mass layoffs, The Elder Scrolls 6 is reportedly set to gain the subtitle Sentinel soon. That's according to a report which also includes some details of where the game that's long been a twinkle in the eye of Skyrim's dad will be set and what its plot will involve.

According to The Verge, The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel could be getting some sort of re-reveal in November that'll lock that in as its full title. Skyrim turns 15 on November 11th, so if Bethesda are looking for a date with some TES significance to it, that one would fit the bill.

Beyond the name, the report points to Hammerfell as the game's setting, something the aforementioned name being confirmed would make obvious if you're an Elder Scrolls nerd like me and know that Sentinel is the name of both a kingdom and city in the Redguards' province. As far as I recall, Hammerfell's also been the setting a majority of fans have believed most likely since that infamous TES 6 teaser in 2018, with some thinking a bit of nearby province and Daggerfall setting High Rock might also be included if the game's map spans the Iliac Bay region.

For now, it's deserty Hammerfell, baby. As for what you'll reportedly be up to there, the report points to The Emma Stones 6 having some secrets to explore linked to the mysterious provenance of the Elder Scrolls themselves. Yep, that's the magic bits of paper which blind people by slamming dangerous and unknowable knowledge into their brains, and can also be used for handy tasks like learning the shout needed to defeat Alduin. You're usually lugging a couple around by the time you've finished TES V, no doubt stuffed between cheese wheels in your massive backpack.

All in all, nothing I can see seems to suggest The Elder Scrolls 6 will deviate much from the sort of adventure Skyrim seemed to be teeing up, with the Thalmor-led Aldmeri Dominion on the march to conquer Tamriel and possibly get up to some metaphysical bollocks to return the land to a state resembling a previous era when elves were on top, if theories long-discussed among fans turn out not to be bunkum.

Such a setup would mirror what Skyrim co-lead designer Kurt Kuhlmann outlined earlier this year as the starting point for the direction he might've taken the game, if he'd helmed it rather than departing Bethesda in 2023.

To be honest, the only thing - aside from the Microsoft stink the game can't escape - that's giving me pause in getting too excited about the direction TES 6 seems to be headed in is that fact that the series' world has been left standing still for so long following Skyrim. I'm not saying it needs a reboot, but I am concerned that - ironically given the Elder Scrolls themselves are time-centric artifacts - this might feel like a game a bit out of time unless it can take a big step mechanically.

#4142. It sounds like you shouldn't expect Destiny 2's campaign unvaulting to be ready until 2028, as Bungie tease their plans for the future of the series

When Bungie announced that they would be ceasing to work on major updates for Destiny 2 earlier this year, it obviously felt like that was the end of that, and any future games were not guaranteed whatsoever. Then last month, they announced that they'll be bringing back all of the shooter's vaulted campaigns, which is obviously a lot of work! Now, in a blog post, the developer has outlined where they're at with this process, offering up a timeline of when to expect the unvaulted campaigns, what will be included with them, and light teases for whatever comes after that.

"Our first pass for unvaulting, available to all players, focuses on getting our campaign slate whole again," head of product Josh Deane explains in the blog post. "We're specifically targeting the activity content of Campaigns, Strikes, and Raids from vaulted expansions. Menagerie holds a special place in our hearts (and we've seen years of community requests for a return), so it will be a part of this pass as well." In practical terms, that means the return of the Red War, Forsaken, Curse of Osiris and Warmind campaigns, strikes, raids and raid lairs from said campaigns, and Menagerie Activity with reprised rewards.

The process for this unvaulting apparently began in June as the team scoped the feasibility of it all, and as of now it's pre-production. Full-on production is expected to start in February 2027 at the latest, but it's worth noting that this is expected to take about 12 months to wrap up. That means you won't be jumping back into any of these beloved expansions until 2028 at least, by the sounds of things.

The team also has "stretch goals" that they're investigating for either the unvaulting launch or sometime after, specifically for things like free roam destinations, seasonal activities from Sundial (season 9) to The Coil (season 32), raid and raid lair weapon updates, and PvP maps.

There are seemingly bigger plans for the game too, with some kind of "celebration" to come beyond Moment of Triumph with "new updates", and something referred to as Destiny 'Legacy'; "Our epic journey started over a decade ago, and the whole experience needs to be served to you all where you play today. Expect more information when we come back to you all early next year." Certainly sounds like they're talking about the original Destiny here, but I suppose we should take that with a pinch of salt. Lastly, they mention "Redacted," which is accompanied by this line, "Launch Ventrilo Message: 'We’re back'". No idea what that means, I'll leave that to you Destiny-heads.

Essentially, the core message seems to be that Bungie are "building a new future for Destiny," so, it's not totally dead in the water. You can expect the next major comms update from Bungie in February, too.

#4141. 'The Best RPG I've Played This Year' - Queen's Domain Is A Low-Key GOTY Contender On Xbox

Back at the end of last month, a little-known RPG launched on Xbox in the form of Queen's Domain, which we highlighted in our October 30th new releases roundup alongside 14 other titles that arrived that day.

Ever since then, we've been hearing various bits of praise for the game across multiple platforms, and it's gotten to the point where it's definitely a Game of the Year contender - albeit a very low-key one.

Officially, what you're getting here is a "retro-fantasy action RPG with brutal combat and traversal-focused exploration", and Queen's Domain is being compared to loads of legendary franchises including King's Field, Zelda and Dark Souls.

Here's what just a few people are saying about it on Steam, for example:

cautious asparagus on Steam: "It's the kind of game that keeps surprising you with the sheer scope and creativity. You know the first time in Elden Ring where you find the elevator that brings you down to Siofra River, and you're just in awe of how much more there is to the game? There are multiple times in Queen's Domain where you feel that same way. This is the best RPG I have played this year, and it might even be my game of the year."

Huell Babineaux: "Everyone says this is one of the best kings field successors out there and it probably is, but ive never played those games, so to me this game feels more like a dark and gritty first person legend of zelda, and it pulls this off exceptionally well. Combat is brutal and unforgiving, but also learnable. Exploration can be daunting and overwhelming, but always rewarding.

Powersteve on Steam: My game of the year. Not just the best King's Field imitator but a genuine improvement on the formula. Better combat, better variety of combat options and a massive world with some of the best level and secret design I have ever seen. Also remains engaging and balanced for the whole duration and doesn't turn into Doom with lightning bolts half way through like Lunacid. So good that I can't wait to get all the endings just so I can use those secrets to do a fresh run with sequence breaks which is something that I almost never do.

So, why haven't we mentioned this before? Well, the Xbox version of Queen's Domain was actually getting a bit of flack at launch, as people were pointing out a stuttering issue that seemed to be plaguing the Series X and S versions.

Looking at the reviews on the Xbox Store now though, the issue seems to have been addressed in a recent patch, and Queen's Domain is currently rocking a 4.7/5 rating on the US version of the Xbox Store as things stand.

In other words, this might well be worth picking up for your Xbox console! It's £16.74 / $19.99 if you fancy taking a punt in the near future, and we'll leave you with more details and screenshots for it down below.

Queen’s Domain is a retro-fantasy action RPG. Washed up on the shores of the Isle of Neasied, you set out to find your father and uncover the dark heart of this mysterious isle. Wield the Legendary Holy Sword Endu to take flight from platform to platform, and discover an interconnected, labyrinthine world where secrets and dangers lurk around every corner.

Fight action-oriented battles with a classic stamina meter, powerful charge attacks, weapon specific special attacks, and secondary throwing weapons. Level up, accessorize, and choose from a huge catalogue of melee weapons on your quest to fight your way through the hordes of monsters and powerful bosses awaiting you in the darkest depths of the isle.

#4140. After the rough start that was last year's entry, Football Manager 27 is looking to bring you in with a few free days of play before the game's even out

Football Manager 27 is still a good week and ahead out from launch, but if you're quick you can already get to playing it. That's because developer Sports Interactive have released a Launch Preview version of the game that lets you take it for a kickabout before it comes out in earnest.

As the devs explain in a Steam blog post, "running for the next five days, the FM27 Launch Preview will be freely playable," across all of its release platforms. "There’s no additional sign-up required, simply download from your preferred platform and begin turning your football vision into dugout decisions. This is your chance to get hands-on with the complete FM27 experience across all game modes, including Shuffle Draft, the fast-paced new multiplayer addition."

One caveat worth noting is that there may be some bugs or glitches in the game that the devs "will work to address in future updates." This, understandably, may be a touchy subject for some. It didn't exactly have a stellar launch, with early patches having to fix hundreds of bugs and other issues. Not that Steam reviews are the be all, end all, but the game is still sitting at a mostly negative a year on. It's very well possible that getting the new one in folks' hands early is a way to bring back some of the audience they may have lost last year.

Still, it doesn't sound like Football Manager 26 was all bad. Phil spent a lofty 227 hours on the game around when it launched, writing for RPS at the time, "That massive database of players, staff and clubs, layered so expertly over time with systems that make them all feel alive and dynamic, is still thrilling. It’s not a new feature by any stretch, but it feels overly punitive to discount it because the menus are bad and it chugs along whenever you press continue. It’s a bad version of a fundamentally great experience, and that means my brain’s going to be full of AS Roma matters for the foreseeable, no matter how many AI gravestones I see in my feed decrying the death of the series."

#4138. Making a $300 PS5 Instead of a $1,200 PS6 Would Be 'True Innovation', Says Ex-PlayStation Boss

As the PS5 generation approaches its sixth year, talk of what comes next has been circulating for a while, and with hardware as pricey as it is, the prospect of a PS6 isn't as exciting as it perhaps should be.

Opinion differs on that, of course, but it's generally accepted that Sony's next-gen machine is going to be eye-wateringly expensive, and it's currently anyone's guess as to whether it'll be worth a purchase.

Shawn Layden, formerly CEO of PlayStation and head of PlayStation Studios, has weighed in on the matter of next generation console hardware in a new interview.

Speaking on the Trophy Room podcast, he says Sony's best move wouldn't be to create a pricey, brand new console, it would be to revise the current hardware in order to sell it cheaper.

"The typical runway for platforms [is] six to eight years, you get a new one," Layden says. "But typically, that new one brought you something mind-blowing."

He speaks about the various innovative leaps from one console to the next, concluding that the move from PS4 to PS5 was mostly led by raytracing and teraflops. He expects technical aspects like this will be used to sell PS6 as well, but says these are "differences only dogs can hear", implying diminishing returns.

"We have enough power in the machine. The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1200, it's to make another PS5 for $300. Now that would be true innovation."

As Layden points out, the current generation is the first to go up in price rather than down, and he thinks continuing with a PS6 at such a premium price point, and focusing on incremental increases in power, risks alienating the audience.

"What the company needs to do is do what it's never done, which is, don't iterate the console," he says. "Make it smaller, make it cheaper, do all the things you can around that. The silicon is fine, the OS is fine. It's more than enough power to build the kind of games all of us want to play."

While his words of wisdom may ring true for many, Sony itself is forging ahead with its next-gen plans, so we'll likely be faced with a costly new console within the next couple of years.

#4137. "We didn't want the brooding hero out for revenge": How quiet lulls and a bird-sketching lead make Control Resonant a more introspective kind of action game

Like the repeating pattern effect afflicting its warped Manhattan, Control Resonant threw me for a loop. One minute I would be brutally slashing and smashing my way through hordes of inhuman enemies, enacting a never-ending chain combo of bellowing violence with my Aberrant, and the next minute I would be scanning nearby rooftops for signs of a squeaking purple dragon plushie to give to a very wiggly dog (who, I was pretty sure, could teleport). Combat often felt desperate and bloody; knockdown-and-drag-out brawls that had me limping away like John Wick after a particularly messy gunkata affair. Still, these fights all ended eventually, and in their place was not always more action-RPG battling but, more often, an odd sense of melancholic peace and quiet. It’s a strange dichotomy I’ve been thinking about nearly nonstop since I finished my first playthrough.

Spoilers/Revelations for Control Resonant ahead. Don’t say we didn’t warn/notify you.

Control Resonant is, as has been extensivly documented and commented upon, a very different game to the original Control. But beyond the most obvious action differences (Jesse packs heat while Dylan speaks softly, carrying a big stick), Resonant seems much more inclined towards these quieter moments. For one thing, the lack of enemy mob respawns, outside of specific major plot beats and world-resetting boss victories, gave me the time to breathe and take in my surroundings in a way Control never let me do. The Oldest House was disorienting by design, and it used the constant Hiss pressure to keep me motivated, always moving towards the next objective or plot point. Control Resonant, conversely, allows the mind to wander.

This makes sense when you look at who you're playing as. A more introspective adventure is the perfect speed for Dylan, someone trained from childhood to be capable of superhuman violence, and is now equipped with the perfect, shapeshifting tool for the job - yet spends one of his first scenes in Resonant enjoying the fresh, crisp Autumn stink of New York City for the first time in his life. When he stumbles out of the Oldest House right at the beginning of the game, the camera shifting focus to a single leaf, floating on the wind to greet him a la Forrest Gump while the dreamy strings and flutes of Petri Alanko’s soundtrack play wistfully behind it, we don't see a killer unleashed. We see a prisoner liberated, and are invited to feel with him the elation that came with finally being truly free. Even if it's coupled with the sadness and conflict of knowing, with his sister missing and Manhattan in danger, he can't simply disappear into the ether.

"We agreed on his direction early," Control Resonant director Mikael Kasurinen tells me. "We didn’t want the brooding hero out for revenge. We wanted someone who doesn’t reach for violence as the first solution, someone who can see beauty where others see horror. He feels empathy for the monsters because he sees himself in them."

Even though much of Control let us in on Jesse’s running inner monologue, I wouldn’t classify it as a very introspective narrative, because Jesse isn’t a very introspective person. She’s motivated by action, living in the moment, constantly moving forward, and this is reflected in the way her and her brother’s story is told in that first game. Jesse would come across a document, a recording, some evidence of the FBC’s abusive treatment of Dylan, and she would feel genuinely terrible about this - but only momentarily, her innate sense of urgency almost forcing her to put her thoughts on hold until the latest threat is dealt with. And even when she does react, she's rarely truly surprised, having known for ages that these were the shadowy G-men who stole Dylan away; any new information mainly just reinforces her existing motivation to find and rescue him.

By contrast, Control Resonant is almost primarily about Dylan’s interiority: his guilt, his need to atone, and ultimately, who he is outside of the clutches of both the FBC and the Hiss. This also reflects on the exterior, in the way the game ebbs and flows between cavalcades of carnage and the many quiet, pensive moments throughout.

"The contradiction is that he has no doubts about himself as a parautilitarian," Kasurinen says. "He knows he can face the paranatural threats and win. What he doubts is whether he deserves to exist as a person. He also has a gentle heart. He wants to help, and he has no trouble saying what he sees and feels."

A perfect example of this type of moment happens in the Sinkhole, a particularly intense, Earth-piercing concentration of the citywide Patterning. The trip to the bottom, using an ad-hoc "diving bell" of cobbled-together FBC sensors, comprises multiple levels of tricky fight scenes, as dozens of crimson fiends coagulate around you in increasingly abstract-looking patterned apartment blocks. The Hiss are brutal here, and you have to work quickly to dispatch each new wave or risk getting overwhelmed. Upon finally reaching the bottom, you’re faced with one more crushing attack, including one massive, flying monstrosity you've likely never faced before. The fight is hard, and tense, but eventually you prevail - only for your diving bell to be yanked back up to the surface, leaving you behind. A diver trapped at the bottom of a paranatural Mariana Trench.

Control Resonant never tells you outright how to escape the subsequent maze; it just lets you navigate the strange geometry and variable gravity on your own, leaving you alone - despite the attempts of handler Zoe to raise you on the radio - with your thoughts. Music rings out, and it’s unclear whether it’s something Zoe is playing for you or if it’s happening in your head, especially as crackling snippets of comms chatter reveal that your minutes stuck in the Sinkhole have lasted hours on the surface.

It's a powerful sequence, heightening the struggle of escape with the dread of hearing how the world is going by outside. And it works because, even with the music, it's quiet enough for you to focus on those feelings. It's a big moment for Dylan as a character, too. He's spent most of his life helpless, first as a 'guest' of the FBC, then as a brainwashed agent of the Hiss. Threatened with entombment in a reality-breaking pit, his voice wobbles with fear, yet he chooses - for one of the first times in decades - to reject that helplessness and save himself. He weighs up those doubts, and decides he deserves to exist.

I still have thoughts on Control Resonant that I haven't reconciled, especially around Jesse. The first female main protagonist of a Remedy game, she does end up sidelined in favor of exploring the inner workings of her brother, including through a series of quests where she risks being literally erased by the Patterning. Then there's the ending that (seriously, spoiler re-warning) has her pull a kind of messed-up UNO reverse card on Dylan's ultimate sacrifice, ensuring that he lives while she... ends up where Dylan had been, all the way back at the beginning of the game. What do we do with this?

"It’s too early to talk about the future," Kasurinen replies when I ask if we might get a new glimpse of the Fadens soon; perhaps a peek at a 'Control: Gestalt,' if you will. Thoughh... yeah, for sure, of course. "But thematically I wanted the two games to complement each other and show two different sides of the same world. The world stays the same, but we see it through a new protagonist."

As someone who played through Control quite thoroughly a few years ago, I didn’t initially feel like I needed a whole lot of extra information about the myriad ways Casper Darling was a wretched manipulator who’d abused Dylan. But on the other side of this, I was occasionally quite taken by the lengths Control Resonant went to give Dylan chances to heal on-screen, whether it was by befriending a dog, hearing new music for the first time since childhood (courtesy of music fan and radio misappropriator Zoe), or drawing perfect still-life tableaus out of piles of garbage he found, ruminating on the idyllic scenes he imagined as he sketched and thinking about how he’d like to experience them once the Altered World Event was over. One drawing, which was just a self-portrait of Dylan in his 40s, sitting on a bench surrounded by birds, hit me profoundly. There is something powerful about imagining a peaceful future for yourself when all evidence has always pointed to the contrary, and there's no better time to have those thoughts than in a moment of quiet.

#4136. Phantom Blade Zero kicks off its launch with a day one patch that offers improvements to ray tracing and some bug fixes to boot

If you've been hankering for some video gamey wuxia shenanigans, today seems like a good day for it, given that Phantom Blade Zero has now been released unto the world (with a 145GB install size that's technically actually 300GB but only for a bit). And like many big games before it, it comes not quite finished, as a day one patch attends to some of the action game's issues… I think, anyway, there's been a promise of a day one patch but no clear indicator if it's actually arrived or not. I don't own it either, so I can't check. At least I can tell you what's in it!

According to this Steam blog post, the update adds on a whole extra 5GB, claiming to significantly improve "ray tracing and path tracing performance," and offer "several bug fixes. If you’ve already pre-loaded the game, please download and install the update before launching. If you haven’t pre-loaded, your download will automatically include the latest version." That does more or less make it sounds like the patch is already here, there just aren't any patch notes to go with it.

The post goes on to explain that the team has "spent a great deal of time refining the game’s rasterized visuals so that each environment stays true to our art direction even with ray tracing turned off." It should also work on mid-range and lower-end PCs, and handhelds too, though on the game's discussions page and elsewhere I have spotted some folks facing some trouble.

Last point on the post also states that they've "observed some performance instability with NVIDIA’s latest 621.01 driver. Based on our testing, version 617.42 currently offers the best experience in Phantom Blade Zero. If you’ve installed a driver newer than 617.42, we recommend rolling back to 617.42 and choosing the clean installation option. Please stay on this version until NVIDIA releases its next driver update, which we expect to arrive soon."

Essentially, nothing that sounds like a massive dealbreaker just yet, so, happy Phantom Blade Zeroing I guess!

#4135. 'The Biggest Launch In WoW History' - Xbox's Latest First-Party Game Is Already Smashing Records

Bodes well for that eventual console release, eh?

We've talked quite a bit recently about the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever on PC and how it may end up being the biggest success of the year from an Xbox first-party perspective, and it seems that could actually be the case.

Its PC launch happened back on November 4th, and according to the folks at The Game Business, it's already broken multiple records for the series, including the biggest launch in WoW history based on peak concurrent players.

Here's a look at those records that have been broken:

Many people might overlook the success of WoW: Forever for Team Xbox simply because it's not shipping on consoles (at least not yet), but we reckon Xbox CEO Asha Sharma will extremely pleased by the game's success thus far!

It does seem to bode well for an Xbox Series X|S and/or Xbox Project Helix version in the future too - there's seemingly little point leaving money on the table when the new game is already optimised for controllers as it is.

Obviously it's still early days for WoW: Forever and the initial success will inevitibly drop off, but if they can retain enough interest in the months and years to come, Xbox will have an excellent new money spinner on their hands.

#4134. Mouthwashing is getting a feature film adaptation from Sony and I need all of you to be normal about it whenever it comes out

I quite liked that there video game Mouthwashing. It had a lot to say about how corporations take advantage of their workers, it played around with character perspective to let you in on certain narrative threads and withhold others until they're taut enough to snap, and was short enough so that its misery didn't outstay its welcome. What I wasn't so fond of was much of the fandom response that came afterwards, which is why I am quite scared to say that it's getting a movie from Sony.

As shared by The Hollywood Reporter, Sony have acquired the feature film rights to Mouthwashing, attaching names both promising and apprehension inducing to it. It's being produced in part by Scott Derrickson, director of Sinister (which I liked well enough) and Doctor Strange (a wet fart sound of a movie). What is more interesting is that Karyn Kusama, director of the excellent cult classic Jennifer's Body, is attached to direct. Given the game's themes of sexual assault, which is putting it lightly, it's nice to see a woman in the director's seat.

YES, MOUTHWASHING MOVIE IS REALLY HAPPENING SOON™ You thought you could escape responsibility by turning off your console? Produced by Sony Pictures' Screen Gems and directed by Karyn Kusama.[image or embed]

The thing that loops me back around to fear is having Matt Manfredi and Phil Hay attached as writers; the pair have long worked together, but often on stinkers like Clash of the Titans, The Tuxedo, and R.I.P.D. At the very least the two of them and Kusama are frequent collaborators, having made The Invitation and Destroyer together (it probably helps that Hay and Kusama are married).

As with every single live action adaptation of a video game, I of course immediately feel that it is wholly unnecessary, and certainly think that's the case for Mouthwashing. It's a game that has minimal interactivity, much more of a walking sim than anything else. It also deeply relies on said interactivity, alongside its first-person perspective, so I'm not sure how well that would translate. And upsettingly, the game developed an uncomfortably intense fandom that has frequently treated the game's themes as a suggestion, prioritising skits and memes above a real reckoning with what it's doing. This leaves me afraid of a film adaptation. Perhaps I'll log off for the day whenever it comes out.

#4131. Baldur's Gate 3 custom campaign mod channels World of Warcraft with an adventure about undead former slaves fighting to reclaim a kingdom

From the creator of the Act Two Expansion mod which came out in September

The opening act of a Baldur's Gate 3 custom campaign mod which injects an adventure set in the World of Warcraft universe into Larian's RPG has been released. The mod, Forsaken, is another ambitious bit of work from a modder who recently expanded the second act of BG3's main story with a new region to explore before you head into the final chapter. This time, they've abandoned the D&Dverse for a tale of undead slaves rising up after being freed from serving a Lich King.

"You play as one of the Forsaken; an Undead who has recently awakened to find they are no longer slaves to the Lich King," modder SquallyDaBeanz wrote of Forsaken, their latest creation to release via Nexus Mods. "Now you must find your place in this new world alongside other freed Undead as you fight to reclaim the kingdom of Lordaeron. Hunt fierce beasts, explore forgotten ruins, end dark rituals, slay zealots, discover magical items, and more in this Custom Campaign for levels 1-5."

This campaign's setting is based on the Tirisfal Glades region seen in both World of Warcraft's classic and vanilla versions, with the mod being deliberately disconnected from the world of Baldur's Gate and SquallyDaBeanz even having aimed to emulate WOW's design philosophy. The initial release only features Forsaken's first act, but there's still plenty to do within that.

More than 20 quests await across a map that the modder said is designed to feel as expansive as World of Warcraft usually does, while offering a good deal of things to discover despite it not being as tightly packed with locations and secrets as vanilla BG3's professionally crafted locales. There are some towns, settlements, and dungeons to run across as you adventure with a party of up to three specially-built companions. The trio - a fighter named Darnell, a mage called Isabella and a cleric named Duesten - can be found in a charming-sounding place dubbed Deathknell Chapel. "The current implementation is temporary and exists purely to have a full party for combat encounters," SquallyDaBeanz noted of these companions. "A complete overhaul is in the works but I chose to put it off for a future update."

While there are NPCs and traders to chat with, the current version of the mod's quite heavily focused on combat and is fairly linear compared to vanilla BG3. Though, that has seemed to be the case with a lot of BG3 custom campaign mods I've covered thus far, especially those that are still works-in-progress like Forsaken.

Going forwards, SquallyDaBeanz hasn't provided an estimate as to when the mod'll be getting a second act, but has laid out some features they plan to add to the opening act in future. More quests, class dialogue, skill checks, items, and lore books are all on the to-do list, as well as adding idle animations and cutscenes for some NPCs.

If you fancy giving Forsaken a go, you'll need to nab its main file and install it with help from the instructions in the mod's description. Then, once you've enabled Forsaken via BG3's in-game mod manager found in the main menu, you'll need to start a new game to be whisked off to WOWville.

#4129. There are no more Assassin's Creed remakes in development, because Ubisoft are focused on Hexe, Invictus and "projects you haven't heard about yet"

They're still updating Black Flag Resynced, however, and bringing NG+ to Valhalla

Ubisoft have announced that they aren't working on any more Assassin's Creed remakes for the moment, despite learning a "tremendous amount" from Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced. Instead, it's all shoulders to the wheel for a thrilling future that contains witches, a stronger sense of narrative cohesion, and possibly some kind of Assassin's Creed Smash Bros equivalent. In the shorter term, Ubisoft are still adding things to both Resynced and Assassin's Creed Valhalla.

The news comes as part of a fireside chat from Jean Guesdon, head of content. After offering libations to Assassin's Creed's new leadership team - in particular Martin Schelling, former Assassin's Creed: Revelations producer and nowadays, head of brand – he shares the results of a survey about whatpeople currently want from Assassin's Creed at large. Ubisoft's three takeaways are that players would like them to communicate more, work harder to shore up Assassin's Creed's "unique identity", and create "a more coherent narrative that respects and expands Assassin's Creed's lore."

All of which is basically telling us nothing, though I'm interested to hear thoughts from old AC stalwarts about where the frame story of Assassin vs Templar has gone off the rails. I feel like "incoherent" is AC's default state and a significant part of its charm. Ubisoft are going to do further closed-doors workshops about the future of the series with certain big cheeses in the AC fanbase, via Discord.

The post includes news of changes to existing Assassin's Creeds. Black Flag Resynced has just been updated with a New Game+ mode, a "nightmare" difficulty setting, some takedown animations, and some fresh cosmetics. Resynced's older/younger sibling Assassin's Creed Valhalla is also getting a New Game+ mode, out 5th November, which introduces a new optional progression system, more resources for upgrades, a new gear quality level, a stash system, and some cosmetics.

There's a section on Codename Invictus, Ubisoft's unrevealed multiplayer Assassin's Creed project, which had a closed playtest featuring a new prototype a few months ago. Ubisoft say people like the PvP, parkour, map verticality, and range of AC characters.

"One piece of feedback came through clearly though: players saw great potential in the foundations but wanted more of the pillars that define Assassin's Creed," Guesdon writes. "The team spent the past months acting on it, and Invictus is now evolving in an exciting direction that better reflects those pillars while staying true to its multiplayer ambitions." I quite enjoyed Assassin's Creed's first efforts at multiplayer, in which players posed as NPCs on crowded maps, but as a Doubting Thomas, I also suspect Invictus is some kind of suffocating live service kraken. I suspect this is what the unnamed playtesters meant by wanting "more of the pillars".

I am more interested to hear about Codename Hexe, Ubisoft's other big forthcoming Creedojaunt, even though Clint Hocking is no longer working on it. It's reportedly a witch fable set during the time of the Holy Roman Empire. They'll be telling us more about that next year, Guesdon says.

Finally - well, apart from some flannel about the AC Netflix series and the series' 20th anniversary next year - there's a paragraph about remakes. "One thing we want to be transparent about today is that we currently have no other Assassin's Creed remake actively in development," Guesdon writes. "Our teams are already focused on the next chapter of Assassin's Creed titles, including projects you haven't heard about yet, featuring new settings and stories. But don't mistake that for a closed door. Like many of you, we love the idea of revisiting our classic titles, and we'll keep exploring opportunities to bring older titles back."

Some context for all this: Ubisoft recently made layoffs at Resynced studio Ubisoft Singapore, in the course of wider cost-cutting after an injection of funds from Tencent. In May, company boss Yves Guillemot told investors that the coming financial year would be a "low point", promising healthier returns from Assassin's Creed, Far Cry and Ghost Recon by early 2029.

I didn't play Resynced, and I'm mixed on remakes at large. I like remakes when they are effectively brand new games that happen to be retelling a familiar story, and having fun with it: games like Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, which are in ferocious dialogue with the original. But remakes that are just about stuffing the mechanics into Unreal Engine 5 and grafting on some progression and crafting mechanics? It's just feeding ash to the fire. What's your mileage?

#4128. A sequel to underrated 2007 Stephen King adaptation 1408 is in the works with original stars returning

Join the GamesRadar community for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

19 years later, Samuel L. Jackson and John Cusack are returning for a 1408 sequel

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Almost two decades after the 2007 movie adaptation brought Stephen King's 1999 supernatural novel 1408 to life, a sequel is in the works.

As reported by Variety, the sequel is being led by original director Mikael Håfström, with stars Samuel L. Jackson and John Cusack set to return, though the pair are still negotiating the terms. The upcoming movie has already added two new faces too: Lord of the Rings star Elijah Wood and Stranger Things actor Natalia Dyer.

Based on King's short story of the same name, the movie follows Cusack as a cynical author named Mike Enslin who investigates haunted places. However, Enslin begins to become a believer when he receives a tip about a haunted room at the New York City hotel The Dolphin. Against the advice of hotel manager Gerald Olin, Enslin checks in for the night in room 1408, and the skeptic experiences bizarre events that he cannot explain away this time.

Cusack and Jackson will return as Enslin and Olin, respectively. But the pair won't be leading the sequel. Variety reports that the writer and concierge duo will be secondary characters, with Dyer set to star in the movie. Details about the new characters remain under wraps, but Wood is also expected to play a supporting role.

Cusack's return isn't too surprising, as in 2025, the actor told People that though he has never had "the desire" to make a sequel, the only movie he would return to is 1408. "Just because… I think today, you know, most movies suck," said Cusack.

No plot details have been shared at this time. However, the original movie actually has four endings, two where Mike dies, and two where he reunites with his wife Lily. Due to Cusack returning, we assume that the sequel will be picking up after one of the endings where Mike is still alive. But there is the possibility that Cusack could be returning as a ghost haunting the hotel, just as the writer met many past victims in his hotel room that night. As for Dyer's character, Mike did have a daughter, but she died years before the events of the movie.

Find out where 1408 places on our list of the best Stephen King adaptations, and keep up with all of the other upcoming Stephen King movies and shows on the way.

#4127. Poll: Xbox Turns 25 This Week, But Which Console Generation Had The Best Launch Titles?

This Sunday, Xbox will celebrate 25 years of great games and console experiences. Without giving away just how ancient we are, Fraser and I have been Xbox players since the beginning, enjoying each new generation of Xbox consoles and the games that launched alongside them.

With November 15th drawing closer, we thought we'd look back on each generation's launch lineup and ask for your verdict: which Xbox console had the best launch titles?

Was it the original Xbox, with Halo: Combat Evolved, Project Gotham Racing, and Fuzion Frenzy? How about the Xbox 360, with Condemned: Criminal Origins, Kameo: Elements of Power, and Call of Duty 2? Perhaps the Xbox One, with Ryse: Son of Rome, Dead Rising 3, and Forza Motorsport 5? Or is it the Xbox Series X|S, with Gears Tactics, Forza Horizon 4, and Sea Of Thieves?

#4125. Helldivers 2 boss can "absolutely see" making a game parody of generative AI, but it would need to be "quirky" rather than "doom-laden"

Arrowhead's chief creative officer Johan Pilestedt can well imagine the Helldivers studio developing a videogame that satirises or parodies today's generative AI technology. The game in question wouldn't be a Helldivers project, however, and Pilestedt says it would need to be relatively upbeat, rather than an exercise in feverish despair. This seems like a tall order right now, at least while Tim Sweeney still has access to Twitter.

"AI has been worth parodying since the ‘80s, and I can absolutely see a game where you’re stuck in a world with an AI overlord that’s basically a deity," Pilestedt told me during an interview on the company's future. "But the Automatons already cover our robot enemy needs in Helldivers 2, so if we went there, it would be a new title, and we’d want to frame it in a quirky, fun way rather than a doom-laden one."

The aim to keep things light is consistent, of course, with how Helldivers approaches satire. "Not everyone gets it, but plenty of players love playing along with the joke," Pilestedt commented elsewhere in our chatathon, with regard to how Helldivers portrays fascism. "The humor doesn't hide the message, it delivers it."

While robotic, Helldivers 2's Automatons aren't a commentary on generative AI. They're broadly a spoof of Soviet Russia, red star imagery and all, if Soviet Russia had happened to be populated by Terminators. Based on the secessionist planet of Cyberstan, the Automatons are led by a group of Cyborgs who are waging war partly out of revenge for Super Earth's efforts to "euthanise" them. Still, perhaps there's scope to patch in more present-day parallels and upgrade the Automatons from cosy T-1000 analogues into something redolent of, say, Krafton's plans to use game data for unpiloted weapon systems.

Any satire of genAI Arrowhead make would need to reckon with the fact that Arrowhead appear open to making use of the technology, within limits. “I find that anything that is [an] AI-related debate in the games industry ends up being on both ends of the spectrum," Arrowhead CEO Shams Jorjani told The Game Business in an interview last year. "Either we have Square Enix executives talking about 77% being automated through QA, or we have developers who feel that... the very fabric of their being is being threatened and therefore all AI is bad AI. Maybe could it be that reality is somewhere in the middle?"

Jorjani contrasted fears about job losses to generative AI with less anxious reaction to older automation middleware such as Simplygon, while conceding that Simplygon isn't on the same "massive scale" as generative AI tools. He also stressed that "we need to make sure that we're not stealing people's intellectual property and rights".

Pilestedt didn't share his own opinions about generative AI during our conversation - in his defence, I didn't ask for them specifically. He did, however, talk about why Arrowhead's current unannounced project isn't Helldivers 3 - briefly, they don't want to "reset" the momentum of Helldivers 2.

#4124. Rockstar developer union could end up over 1,600 workers strong and encompass nearly all UK staff below senior management, IWGB claim

Organisers say a successful vote would create "the biggest recognised union in the UK games sector"

As we've previously covered, a vote on recognition of a union made up of UK-based Rockstar Games devs is set to take place around GTA 6's console launch on November 19th. The Independent Workers of Great Britain (IWGB) union, whom the Rockstar staff are working with in their efforts to organise, have now revealed just how many workers the Rockstar could end up encompassing if the recognition vote is successful. It's not a small number.

As reported by Game File, when asked to put a number on their claim that the vote could result in "the biggest recognised union in the UK games sector", the IWGB said that the union’s bargaining unit would be made up of more than 1,600 workers. That, according to the union, is nearly everyone at Rockstar's UK studios below the director level. The director level's typically corpospeak for senior management, or the point at which you go from regular staff to the lowest rungs of the exec ladder which leads all the way up to the biggest of gold-plated desks.

Naturally, this UK Rockstar union won't include Rockstar staff based in other studios across the world, including the US and India. Recent reporting from Bloomberg cited Rockstar's total staff number as being over 4,700 people in 12 places across the globe.

The UK union recognition votes will be held from November 12th, a week before GTA 6's console launch, and November 26th.

"For me, this vote comes down to ensuring employees at Rockstar get honesty and openness surrounding the decisions that affect them," Rockstar Game Workers Union Committee Member Shanti Easton-Steel said in a press release issued by IWBG earlier this week. "When management choices are kept hidden, we can’t properly address issues like the gender pay gap, the uneven and ever-changing policies on overtime pay, or the concerns many co-workers hold around job security post-release."

Also set to come to a head around the time GTA 6 plops onto consoles is the employment tribunal which has seen Rockstar and the IWGB butt heads over the former's decision to fire 34 mostly UK-based staffers last year. Rockstar have accused the fired staff of risking the leaking of confidential info while posting on a Discord server set up by union organisers. The IWGB have accused Rockstar of being motivated by a desire to union bust.
