Welcome to Dungeon Master, PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke.

We love a big RPG dilemma, don't we? Right up until the point where we actually have to make the choice and we stare at our screens for an uncomfortably long time, hoping we'll figure out a way to make a call and not feel absolutely terrible about it later.

For my money, the best—agonising, guilt-inducing—choices are the really personal ones. I love that Mass Effect lets me determine the fate of the galaxy in all these different ways, but it never gives me a reason to care about the rachni, for instance, or the council, so when I have to decide to save them or let them die, it becomes more of an abstract moral choice.

Disco Elysium, then, left me in tatters. It's more personal and intimate than a productive therapy session. There's a card you can read pretty early on, stuck inside a ledger, that opens the wound that Harry worked very hard—by abusing alcohol and drugs—to forget. If you toss it, you never get it back. That was a hard one. Is ignoring it a kind of liberation? Or are you just helping Harry hide from his trauma?

It's effective because it's powerfully relatable. You don't even need to have experienced a cataclysmic breakup to understand Harry in that moment. We've all got shit we'd really love to forget. Self-destructive choices that we made in a heated moment, leaving regret to constantly claw at us.

Relationship drama should be excellent fodder for RPG choices, but that rarely ends up being true. Usually they end up being friction free, but sometimes you'll be walloped with the classic trope of being forced to decide if they live or die—a cheap trick to force us to care about someone, even if they actually suck. Yeah, I'm talking about you, Ash.

That's why Geralt's romantic misadventures are so effective at spitting out challenging conundrums. The best thing about The Witcher 3's approach is that you can choose not to make a decision. It's so rare for games to recognise that indecision is another choice.

I desperately wanted Geralt to be happy. He deserved it. But I could not figure out the best way to go about giving him his happily ever after. The depths of his feelings for Yennefer nudge you towards making sure they have a life together, but god she's toxic. She regularly makes him feel like shit. Triss actually seems to make him happy, but is that just the safe pick?

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

So I never made the choice. I told both of them I loved them, and they left me tied to a bed while they went off to get drunk. My inability to make a choice was the worst choice. But it also ended up feeling poignant—Geralt so often gets in the way of his own happiness.

OK, what about you lot? What's the toughest choice I've had to make in an RPG? Let me know in the comments.

#4060. Venom-toothed Noxious Terminids are soon to infest Helldivers 2, and it's your noble job to sterilise the galaxy for Super Earth

Helldivers 2 isn't slowing down any time soon, and according to Edwin's recent interview with Arrowhead CCO Johan Pilestedt, it'll continue to be Arrowhead's main priority for the future. As if Helldivers 2 wasn't full of enough horrors for our brave Super Earth Helldivers to shoot at for the betterment of galactic democracy, its next update is due to add an entirely new Terminid subspecies, the Noxious Terminids.

First up on are the Noxious Scavengers. These horrible little (see: huge) things skitter around at high speed and are loaded with deadly poison, but are thankfully at least fragile. Liberal use of area-of-effect weapons such as flamethrowers, explosives and flamethrowers are recommended to avoid being overrun by these horse-sized insects. Then there's the Noxious Spewer, which is not only fast like its smaller brethren despite its larger size, but also equipped with a web projectile which locks a Helldiver in place, vulnerable to a fatal bite. Oh, and if you dare shoot its soft underbelly, it violently explodes, with the same web fluid covering a wide area around it. The poison inflicted by these creatures' bites is a new damage over time effect that can blur vision, slow movement, eat away at your health, and make you fear this may be the end for you — so it's a bit like getting the flu (get your jabs!)

HELLDIVERS™ 2 | A Cleaner Galaxy Starts With You Watch on YouTube

This update also makes the change that bug caves can be found across many more worlds across the galaxy, leading troopers down tunnels with limited visibility and claustrophobic dead ends. Super Earth's propaganda, sorry, I mean, guidance, describes the galactic sterilisation program quite simply: locate the invasive species, identify the horrific monsters at the barrel of your flamethrower, and sterilise (burn to cinders). The guidance also, hilariously, includes the line: "Super Earth reminds you that ammunition is cheaper than antivenom." Now, get out there and rid our beautiful democracy of this vile pestilence.

#4059. Forza director, who'd been with Turn 10 for 27 years leaves Microsoft, following studios merger with Playground Games

Dan Greenawalt, director, founder, and vice president at Turn 10 Games, has departed from the studio after spending 27 years as part of the company. This comes as Turn 10 is merged with Playground Games as part of Xbox's mass restructuring initiative that made headlines as it resulted in 3200 layoffs and four studio closures earlier this year.

In a report by The Verge, an internal memo written by Playground Games studio head Trevor Williams states: "Dan Greenawalt has decided that this is the right time for him to retire from Microsoft".

The memo continues: "It's hard to overstate Dan's impact over the past 27 years. From shipping Project Gotham Racing on the original Xbox in 2001 to leading the creation of Forza, founding Turn 10 Studios and appearing so many times on our E3 stage, usually making a dramatic entrance with a supercar in tow – and so much more – we owe tremendous thanks and gratitude to Dan. On behalf of both teams, I would like to thank Dan for his leadership, his support, and his partnership. I wish him well for whatever comes next.".

With Xbox's merger of Playground Games and Turn 10, the developers will be working in collaboration on the Forza and Fable franchises. The final track racer game that Playground Games developed prior to this merger was 2023's Forza Motorsport reboot, a wonderful racer that offered a sweet alternative to the more arcade Forza Horizon series. In Eurogamer's review, the game was described as: "A generous and lavish racer, with thrilling driving, that wants you for the long haul.".

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Decades before GTA 6, Rockstar Games was considering getting a Japanese studio to develop the now-abandoned GTA: Tokyo, according to a former technical director on the series, but he reckons that there's "so much Americana inherent in the IP" that it might not have worked, anyway.

It sounds like we were so close – yet so far – from getting GTA: Tokyo. A trademark for the title was filed by Rockstar owner Take-Two Interactive back in late 2003, after the release of Vice City, but was later listed as abandoned in 2008. Over the years, we've found out the occasional bits of information about it – one anonymous former Rockstar dev allegedly claimed that the scrapping of the idea ultimately "just came down to logistics," with the tasks of mapping out the city and nailing the "cultural satire in terms of what could possibly work in a fitting narrative way in that city" proving rather difficult.

Obbe Vermeij, a former technical director who left Rockstar in 2009, previously indicated that the game "almost actually happened," with another studio in Japan set to handle development, but that the idea of setting a game in "some left-field location for novelty" wouldn't work. Vermeij has now elaborated on this further in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun.

Vermeij admits that the information was "above my pay grade," but that "there were negotiations with studios, and I have a name, but I'm not gonna say it, because then it becomes like a bigger thing than it is, and I'll probably get it wrong, and I don't know how far the negotiations were, how serious it was. I mean, it was definitely serious. It was the plan. But I don't know how close it got to actually happening."

According to Vermeij, Tokyo's story likely would have been set in the present day, or at the very least, a time "not too [far off] – it wasn't, like, sort of the medieval era in Japanese history, or anything. It was definitely not like that." With that said, though, "it definitely had samurai swords in it," he says. Oh, what could have been.

Tokyo wasn't the only city that Rockstar considered doing something with, according to Vermeij. Paris, Moscow, Rio de Janeiro, London, and Istanbul were frequently suggested internally, he says, but he muses that perhaps a full GTA game set outside of the US might not work very well anyway.

"We always decided there was so much Americana inherent in the IP, it would be really hard to make it work in London or anywhere else," he explains. "You know, you needed guns, you needed these larger-than-life characters. It just felt like the game was so much about America, possibly from an outsider's perspective. But that was so much about what the thing was that it wouldn't really have worked in the same way elsewhere."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

That's not to say he wouldn't have liked a Japanese GTA to happen, though. On the conception of the idea, Vermeij wonders if Rockstar co-founders Dan and Sam Houser "were a little annoyed that GTA wasn't as big in Japan as they thought it deserved to be," and therefore "it kind of made sense to get a local studio to do it." Regardless, though, he thinks "it would have been really cool, because you know, a GTA made by somebody else in Japanese culture – that's something I would probably play."

GTA 6 launch files already hint at online multiplayer, PlayStation Store sleuth reports, leading to hopes we won't be waiting for a GTA Online follow-up for long.

#4057. PS5 Now the Only Console without a Digital Game Gifting Option

If even a Nintendo platform has a digital storefront feature and you don't, then you truly are behind the times. The firm notoriously playing catch-up in this space has today confirmed the Nintendo eShop will be receiving the ability to gift digital games.

The PS Store, which will eventually be the only place you can buy new PlayStation games, still doesn't allow it.

Having downloaded a new system update for the Nintendo Switch 2, the groundwork is laid for a Nintendo eShop gifting feature going live next week. You will be able to gift digital games to people within your Nintendo Account family group.

This implementation is a bit more restrictive than what's on Xbox and Steam, where you can gift digital games to anyone on your friends list. The Nintendo Account family group system, meanwhile, is restricted to a maximum of eight members that all share a single online membership to NSO (Nintendo Switch Online).

Despite the Nintendo approach being less expansive than other storefronts, it's better than nothing.

And nothing is all Sony offers in the digital game gifting space.

Feature 8 Ways Sony Must Improve the PS Store for Our All-Digital Future

From January 2028, PlayStation is going entirely digital with game releases, as it's revealed the production of physical copies for new titles will end. As it leans all the way into the digital space, it makes the PS Store the only place you can buy new PS5 (and potentially PS6 by that point) games.

This has put the PS Store under the microscope, as players now judge the only storefront they'll be able to access new PlayStation releases from. The fact that, as of right now, they wouldn't be able to gift games to their family and friends, is an issue. And now, if the Nintendo Switch 2 can support the feature, there are absolutely no excuses Sony can turn to.

It's one improvement we highlighted in a recent feature that PlayStation really should implement. Other enhancements included a better refund policy, the ability to trade and sell digital games, and a loyalty program.

Currently, the only way you could send a PS5, PS4 game to a family member or friend is by buying them PSN vouchers to redeem. By choosing to focus entirely on digital in the future, Sony must implement a gifting feature where the full process is done entirely on the console.

#4056. EA reportedly closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between Mass Effect 5 and Star Wars Battlefront 3

And it chose the "less risky, more predictable bet".

A new report has revealed that EA closed BioWare because it was forced to choose between investing in one of two sci-fi projects: a new Mass Effect game or a new Star Wars Battlefront game. And it chose the latter.

The revelation comes from Bloomberg, which heard from "people familiar with the company's strategy" that the "recent emergence" of an opportunity to develop a third Battlefront game meant EA - a company saddled with $18bn in debt because of the recent leveraged buyout - would have two sci-fi projects, each likely to cost hundreds of millions of dollars to make.

It couldn't afford to make both of them so EA executives chose Star Wars Battlefront 3, because it was seen "as a less risky, more predictable bet than a new Mass Effect", Bloomberg reported - despite development for the game not even having begun yet.

An EA spokesperson said the company had "collectively reached this decision following months of planning, review, and analysis, including careful consideration of evolving business conditions, industry dynamics, and our long-term priorities". "While this is never easy," the spokesperson went on, "we ultimately have to make tough decisions to focus our teams on the biggest opportunities for our future, including investing in new projects across our portfolio."

The report highlights a few other contributing factors in EA's decision, including BioWare's unfavourable recent track record and a reorganisation of its executive ranks to include more EA Sports people, in favour of those advocating for BioWare. EA bosses even lamented Dragon Age: Veilguard's sales, suggesting it would have been better if the title was 'a live service game'.

Last week, following the announcement of BioWare's closure and the cancellation of Mass Effect 5, an internal video for the project - known as Mass Effect Universe - was leaked, showing what appears to be a pre-rendered visualisation of it. The game was said to take place 600 years after the Reaper war, in the midst of a galactic cold war, and to have the player be "a cross between John Wick and James Bond" in terms of what they'd be capable of.

There was a promise of "Hitman-style freedom" in approaching levels, romance that "wasn't being sanitised", and for connections between the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies. It's not clear how much work was done on it, but clearly a lot of planning had been done - far more, certainly, than has been done on Battlefront 3.

EA's Star Wars Battlefront 2 was released in 2017 and struggled, initially, to convince - partly because it was riddled with loot boxes. But years of adjustments and improvements left it in a much better place.

#4055. Frostpunk 2's The Surge DLC keeps the wintery apocalypse and adds in faction-clash-inducing electricity and sets a seasonally appropriate December release date

For the time being, the world of Frostpunk remains a hypothetical, even if it's one that seems just that little bit more likely than I'd like it to be given who's in charge of the world. But at the very least, there are pockets of hope to be found in Frostpunk 2, namely with its newly revealed next bit of DLC, The Surge, a name that has been bequeathed to it for incredibly obvious reasons. Oh, you need me to explain them? Fiiiiine.

You and your probably not so merry band of survivors have been trekking across the UK, when you end up at a "mysterious valley." Apparently some rumours have been going round about a "marvel left behind by history’s greatest mind - a relic with the potential to reshape the world itself." So you go off to look for it, and it essentially seems like this relic lets you use a whole bunch of electricity. Only, despite how useful this is for automating a bunch of work, various factions disagree over how it should be used, "while the secrets hidden within the valley prove far more difficult to uncover than anyone expected."

In terms of what you should expect from this DLC, for starters there's a new scenario to check out "set in an entirely new region, far beyond the borders explored in Frostpunk 2 so far." This relic is also implied to have come from the mind of one Nikola Tesla, you know, the electricity guy. There'll apparently be ways to utilise the Great Storm that's ruined the planet to "turn catastrophic whiteouts into valuable, harvested and stored resources." And you'll have some hidden treasures to find and mysterious to uncover in various nearby caves and ruins.

All sounds neat enough! And it's not too far away either. The Surge is currently slated for a seasonally appropriate December 14th release date. Let's hope no real world environmental disasters get in the way of that, 'ey? While you wait for it, you can wishlist the DLC on Steam.

I'm kinda just playing chiller PvE, here.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've been stuck into World of Warcraft: Forever—at the time of writing, I'm around 15 hours /played (and will likely be 20+ hours by the time you're reading this) on my warrior. I chose the roleplay ruleset because, well, I'm a roleplayer. I've been writing and being cringe in videogames for over 15 years.

RP in WoW is, actually, what got me into writing in the first place. My clear and obvious mastery over the written word was hard-won by being a terribly annoying edgelord death knight, for which I apologise.

I was curious about the implementation of the roleplay ruleset back when it was properly announced—back then, I thought it was great that we're being given our own place, but being completely split off from "normal" ruleset (which I'll be calling PvE for simplicity) didn't seem necessary to me.

Having played in the roleplay ruleset for a little while, my opinion has only been vindicated. Splitting PvE and PvP rulesets does make sense. For instance, a resource node might be easier to gather on PvE, throwing the economic balance of the PvP server out of the window. But beyond technical limitations, a complete, strict divide between RP and PvE just has me scratching my head.

There are things I like about having our own little nook of the Forever servers to putz about on. For starters, the vibes are a lot chiller. I don't want to cast generalisations about players, but I do think roleplayers are just smarter, sexier, have bigger muscles, and will solve climate change.

In seriousness, I do think thinking about your character's place in the world and having a bent towards immersion does make you a chiller person in general. I've experienced vanishingly little toxicity or hostility. The absolute worst instance was a tank getting a little passive-aggressive about mining nodes in my Deadmines run. That's it.

But what I foresaw is bearing out: Nobody is really roleplaying in instanced or group content, and that's because we legitimately never have done so. Most RP takes place either spontaneously out in the open world, or in dedicated hot spots. Even in the most diehard MMO communities, people aren't talking in ye olde English while pushing Vancleef's face in.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

There are some people who are always in-character, sure, but that portion of the playerbase is incredibly rare. We're talking a sliver of an already-small population of a videogame, here.

As for the strict rules on naming conventions—yeah, I'm seeing a lot more lore-accurate names, but I'm also seeing plenty of joke ones. And if I'm being perfectly honest, these gag names really haven't ever bothered me; people being disruptive or annoying when I'm roleplaying are a massive pain, but if Tsundere Cowbell the paladin wants to watch me write, my immersion isn't shattered.

Overall, I think keeping us on our own server architecture for the most part is the smarter plan, especially given layering would dilute roleplayers so much that RP would be hard to find. However, I don't think there's any real reason to disallow us from jumping to the Normal ruleset servers when we group up with someone from there—or giving us an option to travel between them of our own accord.

Just as we tend to swap between in-character for roleplay and out-of-character for, y'know, playing the videogame—I think most of us would be happy to have the choice as to whether we want to futz about on the roleplay layer or go hang out with our non-theatre kid friends on the PvE ruleset.

Especially given, as time goes on, population might become an issue. Believe it or not, roleplayers still do like to raid and gear up, and if they should be able to migrate on characters they've invested literal dozens of hours into, rather than having to start all over again.

#4053. Crimson Desert Enhanced Edition gets a surprise demo on PlayStation and Xbox, lets you play for 5 hours and carry over your save data

Crimson Desert is one of 2026's most successful releases. The game managed to sell over 6 million copies in just three months, and ended up being so profitable that its publisher ended up giving each employee at development studio Pearl Abyss a $3,400 bonus. Since launch, the dev has been committed to improving the game and correcting some of the more egregious issues that were present at launch.

Now, over half a year after its launch - and with the publisher's revenue up a massive 419 percent - it seems the company is eager to let anyone that hasn't yet purchased the game try it out, completely free. To celebrate the launch of the delayed Charting the Unknown DLC, which came out yesterday, Pearl Abyss has made the first five hours of the game completely free to play for (nearly) anyone on Xbox or PlayStation.

Any trial progress you make carries over to the full game if you decide to purchase it, and once your five hours are up, that's it - you can't restart the trial on a different save or something like that. The timer is final.

Charting the Unknown is the first bit of DLC for the game - there's likely more to come - and a Switch 2 version of the sandbox fantasy RPG is currently in development. The developer has hinted at multiplayer-focused DLC in the future, as well as a sequel to the popular game. If you're curious what took the world by storm earlier this year, you can try the free trial on your console of choice right now.

#4052. Play as water and rain on wildfires in Atuel, a short, free game about the power and vulnerability of nature

Well, have you played Atuel? If not, you can do so within the next hour - it's a tiny, free, 25-minute walking sim, albeit one with little actual walking on account of you playing most of it as a river. More of a running sim, really.

Have You Played? is an endless stream of game retrospectives.

Technically, Atuel calls itself a "documentary game", and not without justification. While its sweeping Patagonian landscapes are rendered with a dreamy otherworldliness, and certain moments are downright mystic, the whole watery journey is based directly on the Atuel River that runs through western Argentina. As you drift downhill, taking control of water, clouds, and the local wildlife, you'll hear real-life scientists and historians monologuing on the Atuel and its relationship with the human cultures it's nourished. Mercifully, these are delivered with thoughtfulness as well as earnestness, maintaining the game's contemplative atmosphere without making it sound like the audio guide to a museum of Birmingham canals.

A few bends in, Atuel also takes on the climate crisis, directing you away from the soothing freshwater and into wildfires and parched riverbeds. I'd say this was preaching to the choir, at least for anyone who a) desires a functioning planet and b) learned about the water cycle in primary school, but then it isn't really preaching. Rather, developers Matajuegos weave between the beauty of the Earth and the need to protect it quite gracefully, and end their river tour on a more hopeful note than its darker moments may have intimated.

There's plenty else to leave an outsized impression in your memory matter: the understated, naturally-textured soundtrack, for instance, or the patiently gradual zoom-outs that slowly unveil the Andes' wild splendour. For me, and without wanting to undermine the importance or the accuracy of Atuel's environmental point, it was mainly just nice – therapeutic, even – to float through its gorgeous, surreal scenery like a cloud. And sometimes, as one. You can download it for free from Steam and Itch, with a pay-what-you-want option on the latter.

#4050. Mini Review: Warhammer Survivors (PS5) - Absurdly Addictive Crossover Is a Match Made in Bullet Hell

Warhammer Survivors is exactly what its name suggests: a Warhammer reskin of Vampire Survivors.

Developed by licensed Warhammer studio Auroch Digital, with Vampire Survivors creator poncle partnering on the project, it's a fantastic, heartfelt adaptation right out of the gate.

Indeed, it's immediately obvious that an awful lot of care has been taken in providing poncle's world-beating gameplay formula with a fresh coat of paint. The Warhammer settings, characters, enemies, and weapons are all there — but the game also relishes in dishing out smaller references to Games Workshop's immensely popular fiction.

In particular, I was left pleasantly surprised by how often Warhammer Survivors pays tribute to the property's tabletop identity. Numerous playable characters, for example, are unlocked by finding miniature figure paints scattered across maps.

Meanwhile, power ups can include rolling damage dice — actual dice — across the battlefield, crushing your foes in the process. You can even drop giant blast radius templates on top of your enemies if you're lucky.

What I'm saying is that Auroch Digital and poncle clearly had loads of fun with this one — it's not just a simple copy and paste job that takes advantage of the Warhammer name.

Oh, and it's basically two games in one. On the main menu, you can pick between Warhammer's dark sci-fi 40,000 setting, and its high fantasy Age of Sigmar setting. Each comes with its own character roster, maps, enemy factions, objectives, upgrades, and everything else, making for a seriously robust package.

Gameplay-wise, the title offers a slight twist on the absurdly addictive Survivors structure. Stages have a 25-minute time limit instead of 30, and I'd say there's a larger emphasis on tactical thinking.

That's because specialised opponents are more prevalent, forcing you to weave your way through the hordes in a more methodical manner. At least, until you rack up so many super-powered upgrades that anything in your path just evaporates anyway.

Yep, that same progression curve that makes Vampire Survivors so insanely moreish is alive and well here, although I do think it takes a little longer to hit those truly chaotic highs because of the aforementioned tweaks.

All in all, Warhammer Survivors perfectly melds Games Workshop's property with poncle's timeless formula, resulting in another exceptional roguelike experience.

#4049. Silica, an FPS and RTS hybrid that mixes a smidge of Dune and Helldivers together, has left early access and entered 1.0

The concept of fusing an RTS and an FPS always sounds like a fun one, and since 2023 Martin Melichárek has been trying to make a new take on the combination under the watchful eye of DayZ devs Bohemia Interactive through Silica. Today marks the day that Silica leaves early access and enters 1.0, fully fleshing out its hybrid and mish mash of Dune's Arrakis and Helldivers' Terminids.

Digging into Silica a touch more deeply, it is a sci-fi shooter set on a planet where there's a fancy resource you're trying to mine that definitely isn't the spice. There are two warring factions competing for said resource, when, uh oh! Some bug-ish, giant aliens aren't very happy you're doing all that. So, you can either join the fray on the ground with some classic first-person shooting alongside your friends, or you can take the role of commander and dictate your artillery from above.

The 1.0 update obviously comes with a few additions, namely the Centauri Campaign, a "story-driven single-player experience set in the war for Baltarus. It opens with a cinematic intro and features fully voiced mission briefings and in-game dialogue. Between missions, a 3D planetary globe tracks the war as territory changes hands." Commanding your army should be a better experience now too, with the ability to "arrange units into formations, issue more precise movement and attack orders, and quickly select all units of the same type. Improved AI targeting and vehicle movement also help your armies operate more effectively in large-scale battles."

Beyond that, 1v1 matchmaking has been added in, where you can fight against another commander. The Steam Workshop sandbox tools have been expanded for building your own scenarios and sharing them with others. And there are a whole bunch of bug fixes, quality-of-life improvements and additions, and more. You can read about some of those in more detail in this handy little blog post. If you like what Silica is putting down, then you can pick it up on Steam.

#4048. Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3's online servers are temporarily going dark, FromSoftware announces

Things might get even darker over in the world of Lordran without those silly, only sometimes helpful notes left by other players. Developer FromSoftware has announced that it's temporarily closing Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3 servers because of an unspecified issue.

"Due to a server issue, the game servers for the following titles will be temporarily unavailable on all platforms," the RPG studio tweeted earlier today, before naming Dark Souls 2 and Dark Souls 3.

While the server shutdown won't last forever, FromSoftware hasn't told series fans when exactly they can expect online play to be restored. That presumably means PvP invasions, summon signs and in-game messages that try to troll you off a cliff are unavailable for the time being.

"We will provide updates once we have information regarding the server restoration time. We apologize for the inconvenience," the studio added. I hope you've stocked up on Estus Flasks, at least.

Of course, this isn't the first time the Dark Souls trilogy has had to contend with server problems. In 2022, Bandai Namco took servers for all three Dark Souls games offline due to a security vulnerability affecting Dark Souls 3. The threequel went dark once again a few months later.

FromSoftware's next game The Duskbloods - the one with the jetpacks and vampires and a cute bird thing - hasn't been any luckier, either. The multiplayer-focused game's first network test had to be taken offline early due to similarly vague "server issues". More recently, FromSoftware delayed its Switch 2 exclusive into next year.

"While development of The Duskbloods is at the final adjustment stage, we have made the decision to move the launch window to 2027," the developer tweeted this week. "We apologise to players who have been kindly awaiting the release of this title and thank you for your patience and support."

In a Thursday, November 5 interview with Yahoo Finance (via TechRadar), AMD CEO Lisa Su emphasized the company's AI commitments. Separately, in a Q3 2026 earnings call, Su forecasted an overall "dobule-digit" slump in PC sales in 2027.

"We're a tech company that has a lot of resources and the ability to expand our supply and expand our ability to help our customers. And that's what's led to tremendous growth. So being able to say that my data center business is going to grow 50% sequentially from Q3 to Q4, it's a big step up and it's a testament to how important computing is in the industry today.

"We're looking to double the business⁠—more than double the business⁠—as we go into next year. We are a data center-first company, that is our profile and people need more computing to power all these applications.

[Responding to a question about this past week's slump in AI and tech valuations] "I think the market can sometimes be a little bit short-sighted. Look, it is what it is. What I look at is in the long term, if you believe⁠—which I do, deeply⁠—that computing in many ways equates to intelligence. So the more compute you have, the more intelligent you are, the more intelligent your company is, the more problems you're going to be able to solve, the more you're going to accelerate your business.

"If you believe that foundation, then investing ahead of the curve is the right thing to do because we're always investing for the long term. Long term being, you know, three, four, five years and beyond. And that means you have to make the investments now.

"I've always operated AMD that way. We're always looking at, what do we see over the horizon? And over the horizon, I see AI and super intelligence becoming more and more essential to every aspect of our lives and every aspect of our business. So I believe in this demand and I very much believe that many of the investments that are being made throughout the ecosystem are also seeing some of these same trends."

I found Dr. Su's statements incredibly frustrating, and that all comes down to fundamental differences in perspective and incentive. I do not believe that "computing equates to intelligence" when the output of AI models is so unreliable. They have not changed my life or my work, except to make computer components prohibitively expensive. I do not see "super intelligence" becoming more essential to every aspect of my life in the coming years.

Dr. Su sees the post-US midterm election decline in tech stocks as Mr. Market being short-sighted, but I see overinvestment in data center buildouts and the ludicrous valuation of AI companies as the fundamental error. PC sales will undoubtedly slump next year as the RAMpocalypse continues, but it's hard to swallow tech leaders' sober prognostications on the subject when they caused the shortages and price increases driving the slump.

I believe⁠—and what's more, I hope⁠—that the fever will break and that there will be a correction. Unfortunately, with how much of the economy⁠—particularly 401ks and pension funds⁠—that has been bet on AI's continued growth, I think the coming hangover will be far more democratically distributed than the decision to go on the bender in the first place.

#4046. Blizzard hints at console ports for World of Warcraft: Forever - "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want"

After more than two decades dominating the PC MMO battlefield, it sounds like Blizzard Entertainment's taking the idea of a World of Warcraft console port more seriously than ever.

World of Warcraft: Forever's beta seems to have been immensely popular with fans of the series. It's a brand new third version of the iconic multiplayer game that sits alongside WoW's Classic and Retail portions, and it's recaptured many a lapsed Warcraft sicko with tons of good changes, big and small - one of which is controller support for the first time ever.

Speaking to GamesRadar about the decision to keep World of Warcraft: Forever exclusive to PC players, despite now supporting gamepads, vice president and executive producer Holly Longdale hinted that the fantasy game might just make its way to even more devices and players over time.

"What you just described is really what we're after," she told the outlet. "Play it wherever you want and, at some point, on whatever you want. But the first leg of that journey is getting gamepads working really well with World of Warcraft, and we thought Forever was the perfect place to start."

Longdale reckons all gaming platforms might become "more ubiquitous" in the future, as well. She specifically named the Xbox Project Helix, which is said to be a PC-console hybrid device of some kind. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed the next-gen console can even play your PC games earlier in the year.

"Honestly, we just want to be able to play it anywhere. We've seen people getting it working on the ROG Ally X," Longdale added. "I think just doing some of the work we're doing on gamepad is going to give players a lot of flexibility that I think goes beyond consoles."

World of Warcraft: Forever properly launches on the 4th of November.

Despite struggles in the rest of the Xbox division, Forever's beta was supposedly the "largest" in series history. Elsewhere, Longdale acknowledged that some of the developer's decisions won't make everybody equally happy: "I think the lesson we learned the most over time is 'You don't listen to the loudest people in the room.'"

#4045. The Citadel Project is a Thief-inspired dark fantasy, survival-horror lite stealth-em-up with some lovely shadows set in a medieval megastructure

You know, given the whole stealthy element of Thief-like immersive sims, I'm surprised there haven't been more of them with horror elements. There's Gloomwood, sure, but it's not as common as I'd like. That in turn then makes me curious about The Citadel Project, an immersive sim with some survival-horror elements set in a nasty, parasite-infected dark fantasy world, all apparently made by just one person.

In The Citadel Project, "the last line of defense built by the Ancient Kings in an attempt to preserve what remains of humanity in the face of the Great Storm." Some kind of evil force is ruining it from the inside, and you have to make your way through a medieval megastructure to figure out what happened. You aren't anyone special, "just a simple prisoner who manages to escape from a cell deep within the Citadel." Truthfully, the story sounds fine enough, I'm more smitten with the vibes put on display.

The shadows are what sells me, for the most part. They're dark and moody, looking plenty ripe for hiding in. And look, if you hand me a megastructure to explore, I'm going to do so. I'm also a fan of your main weapon, a crossbow. Not enough games with crossbows if you ask me! There's all sorts of bolts you can use with it, like a fire bolt that, obviously, sets things or enemies alight, a rope bolt to help you quickly climb or swing out of danger, a decoy bolt that makes a lot of sound to distract with, or a moss bolt; I'm not sure what that one does, my guess would be to dampen your footsteps and make it easier to sneak up on unsuspecting baddies.

Said baddies also appear to be infected with some kind of parasite, the severing of which appears to come in handy when trying to take them down. Overall, The Citadel Project likes a neat little im sim with just enough going on to make me curious to explore further. Which I might do, when I get the chance, as there is a demo available on Steam. Alternatively, I could just wait a week, as the game is out in early access November 11th, just over a week away. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

Having spent decades working on Bethesda games, including many of The Elder Scrolls and Fallout releases, Bruce Nesmith knows a thing or three about solid RPG design. Naturally, then, he became enthralled by Baldur's Gate 3 just like the rest of us, largely because of how it rejected principles of his former workplace.

In an interview with The Examined Game, Nesmith discusses what he enjoyed about Larian Studios' take on the world of Dungeons & Dragons. "Bethesda Games have always had the philosophy of, let the player play everything," he explains.

"You can play the entire thieves guild, you can play the entire fighters guild, you can play the entire mages guild, there is nothing your character can't play," he continues. "That's a very good philosophy, I support that philosophy. But I was pleasantly surprised to see how positive it felt to me to make consequential decisions that closed off gameplay in Baldur's Gate 3."

Larian's sprawling fantasy RPG is very decision-focused. Your choices, through dialog and actions, consistently dictate the narrative for you, requiring multiple playthroughs if you want to see every which way the central plot can go.

Morrowind, Oblivion, Skyrim, and Fallouts 3 and 4 are more streamlined, even though there are some forks in the road across each. It's worth highlighting Morrowind here, because you can only join one of the three great houses in the game, introducing some consequences to your actions, but minimally compared to Larian's web of storytelling.

"That felt good, because it was done well," Nesmith goes on. "I felt like the decisions I made had more meaning in certain ways, because there were actual consequences, and if I wanted to see that other gameplay, I'd have to bring up another character and try different paths."

It's no wonder that the average Baldur's Gate 3 playtime on Steam is north of 100 hours. People complete it, then circle back to see what else they can get up to. But the big question now is: Who did Bruce romance? Anyone in the know is free to contact me.

Baldur's Gate 3 has sold over 23m copies and made around $1.2b so far, analyst claims - but only 1% of players have crossed the 500 hour mark in playtime.

#4043. GOTY hopeful Mina the Hollower bought the studio financial stability "for now," while the Shovel Knight devs work on a new 3D game

Yacht Club Games has confirmed that most of its developers are now working on a brand new 3D game (potentially Shovel Knight 3D), after the critically-acclaimed Mina the Hollower did well enough for the team to continue.

Before launching its old-school adventure game earlier this year, Yacht Club described Mina the Hollower as a "make-or-break" moment for the beloved indie studio. A global pandemic and a failed experiment to turn Yacht Club into a multi-project studio had left the developer on thin ice, it seems.

But Mina the Hollower sold well enough to buy the studio more time, according to a new Reddit AMA full of interesting tidbits. Asked if Mina was able to secure financial stability for the company, Sean Velasco simply said "yes… for now!" Mina managed to sell over 500,000 copies in its first two weeks, so it's well on its way to the one million copies the devs were once hoping for.

For the foreseeable future, the devs aren't ready to talk about the kinds of DLC and spin-offs and follow-ups that dear old Shovel Knight enjoyed for many years, but they're not abandoning their newest baby either. "We're working on more post-release features," the devs wrote, which includes "expanded randomizer options, enemy and boss randomization, more modifiers, speedrunner features" and more ways "to do even more in Mina."

Another fan also asked the folks at Yacht Club about their unannounced 3D Shovel Knight game - Velasco previously told Bloomberg that the game was halfway done before the entire studio put all hands on deck for Mina, and pivoted back into a one-game outfit. Alec Faulkner stopped short of confirming Shovel Knight 3D, but said "most of us are currently working on a 3D game, yes!" Alright then, Alec, keep your secrets. "Not sayin more! Other than that it’s gonna be soooooooo awesome."

Co-founder Nick Wozniac went further into the state of the developer, and why splitting the team in half was probably a mistake. Here's what he had to say on the matter: "Sales are the things that keep the company afloat so it's not born from greed (mostly) that we say we'd love to see more sales, it's all about continuing to work together and make great games and reaping the rewards along the way. We are doing ok and learned a lot this cycle. I think we learned mostly that keeping the team tight and focused is what helped Mina land. Splitting the team up to work on two games was something we could have corrected a long time ago but I'm glad to be where we are now. Just gotta pocket those lessons and use them to drive you forward."

Eurogamer's five-star Mina the Hollower review called it an "adventure that takes inspiration from the greats."

#4042. "Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop": Salacious Fire Emblem-ish Food Devils gets a delay because its devs think Valve is inundated with genAI games

You might have seen that for today's grub, Edwin decided to in part feed The Maw with Food Devils, an incredibly salacious, foodie take on Fire Emblem, as it was meant to release today. The only problem is, it's not actually out yet. That might prompt you to call Edwin a rotten liar and march up to his castle at the top of the hill on a dark and stormy night with pitchforks and torches, but I beseech you to wait, because it's actually Steam's fault. And potentially, it's the fault of all those awful AI games that have been flooding Steam recently.

In a Steam blog post shared earlier today, developer Studio Daimon explained why the game isn't able to be released today, first offering a bit of context: if you want to put your game on Steam, you have to submit for approval so that it matches what you've described and doesn't harbour malware, amongst other reasons. As the post explains, "before submitting a build, devs see a disclaimer that says 'This review typically takes 3-5 business days, but please allow up to 7 business days in case feedback needs to be addressed'." Except the team submitted their build on October 12th, more than 20 days ago, with no approval in sight.

The reason? "We can only assume it's because Steam's review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers." For some context, Game Discovery Tool did some statistics magic and found that more than 50% of games released in October on Steam featured an AI disclosure. Valve have required that games disclose AI use since January 2024, and a year on from then in January 2025 only just over 14% of games featured such a disclosure. In January 2026, that jumped up to a little over 25%, and now here we are at more than 50%.

And to be clear, Steam releases have gone up too. According to SteamDB data, a little over 2000 games were released on the platform in October 2025. But in October 2026, that has jumped up to almost 4000. Correlation is obviously not causation, so take that with a pinch of salt. Still, it paints a concerning image over AI usage, and potentially sounds like it's affecting how Valve operates. Almost as if allowing free reign over AI is bad, or something!

Unfortunately for Studio Daimon, there's no estimate on when Food Devils might launch. "Even now, we don't know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game," they wrote. "We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored. I'm sure that their staff is just too overwhelmed at the moment, but these sudden and massive delays have affected many developers throughout October, with some even being forced to postpone their releases... including us."

They're hoping to still be able to release it by the end of the week, but "can't make any plans or promises because it's out of our control." Perhaps in the meantime, for those who like what's cooking in the devs' kitchen, we could throw the game a wishlist to be ready for whenever it does launch.

#4041. Dedicated PS5, PS5 Pro Patch Aims to Fix Silent Hill 2 Graphics Issues

Could the excellent Silent Hill 2 remake finally be fixed on base PS5 and PS5 Pro? That's what a new patch for the game seems to be suggesting.

A new update for the survival horror remake, dedicated entirely to PS5 and PS5 Pro, is live now, bringing it up to version 1.08. The patch notes speak of addressing all the graphical issues that have quietly plagued the game for months now.

Having installed the new update, you should discover "numerous fixes" relating to the "lighting, shadows, and reflections [issues] that were occurring in multiple locations". Both of the Performance and Quality modes have been patched with consistency improvements, and the flickering in water surfaces, lighting effects, and reflections has been "corrected".

While these were not major problems, the patch also improves the cutscenes in certain places and fixes a glitch where you wouldn't be able to obtain some items.

The issues surrounding Silent Hill 2 — the PS5 Pro version in particular — date all the way back to a month after the original release. At the time, Bloober Team was aware of the problems and a patch was being worked on. The update didn't work, and eventually, the responsibility shifted to publisher Konami. More updates followed, and now today's new patch 1.08 directly targets PS5 and PS5 Pro fixes.

"Not since the infamous debut of Daikatana has the release of a single game generated so much incensed indignation from early buyers." Our review of Pool of Radiance: Ruins of Myth Drannor didn't hold back. The 2001 dungeon crawler contained, our review said, "A multitude of outrageous bugs," including ones that corrupted saves, made quest items disappear, and most infamously deleted system files when you uninstalled the game.

SNEG's rerelease, available now on Steam and GOG, doesn't have those issues. It adds widescreen, controller support, adjustable combat speed, tooltips, an action bar, and sharpened visuals. If, like me, you skipped this one back in the day because of its reputation for being a hassle to play—even with the eventual patches and community fixes—now it's smooth and problem-free. I've played the opening hours without a single key item vanishing or save file going corrupt.

Don't get the wrong idea, though. Ruins of Myth Drannor isn't Vampire: The Masquerade – Bloodlines. This isn't an RPG masterpiece held back by its buggy release. It's a simplistic turn-based dungeon crawl that's mostly notable for being a spiritual successor to the first Gold Box D&D game, Pool of Radiance, and for adapting the then-new third edition of D&D's rules.

The 3.0 rules were a huge step forward at the time. Any character could choose any class, and Armor Class went up instead of down—you can't imagine how much of a drag it was explaining to new players that lower AC was better than high AC, and ideally you wanted a negative number. It also formalized the central mechanic of rolling a d20 and adding a number to beat a difficulty score. If you've played 5th edition, you'll recognize a lot of its DNA here.

Which is why it's a shame Ruins of Myth Drannor isn't a complete adaptation of those rules. You can't play a wizard—sorcerer is the only option for arcane casters—or a halfling or a gnome. You choose which class to improve when you advance a level, but don't get to decide where your skill points go or what feats to take. A couple of years later, The Temple of Elemental Evil would adapt the 3.5 rules update much more fully. Ruins of Myth Drannor feels rudimentary by comparison.

It's also not much of a story. Set 10 years after the events of Pool of Radiance, a new magical pool has opened in the ruined elven city of Myth Drannor so the evil sorceress and dracolich on the box art can get up to some shenanigans, and Elminster has sent a party of adventurers in to stop them. There's one fun twist to this otherwise bog-standard plot, and it's that you're not that first party of adventurers. You're the B-team sent as backup, but a magic portal mishap means you arrive too late to save the A-team and have to take on their quest.

Which explains why four level-one nobodies now have to clear out hundreds of orcs and skeletons from samey dungeon rooms. It's a slow-paced slog, especially in Myth Drannor's main halls, earning a drip-feed of experience points and gold coins from zombies and ghouls, hoping an orc doesn't score a crit and drop one of your party members in a single blow.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

There are plenty of reasons not to like Ruins of Myth Drannor, but I've been enjoying it in spite of them. It's an undemanding RPG that offers simple pleasures. I get ambushed by skeletons, then realize my cleric is perfectly positioned to hit them all with Turn Undead. I meet a weird slug monster, try talking to him and find out he's friendly. I block doors to protect my sorcerer, while rushing enemy spellcasters before they get their big area-of-effect blast off.

It's junk food D&D, but then I mostly play D&D at a table covered in pizza and beer anyway. Between more demanding games, this is an ideal low-stakes guilty pleasure and I'm glad it's finally back.

Jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. A former music journalist who interviewed everyone from Giorgio Moroder to Trent Reznor, Jody also co-hosted Australia's first radio show about videogames, Zed Games. He's written for Rock Paper Shotgun, The Big Issue, GamesRadar, Zam, Glixel, Five Out of Ten Magazine, and Playboy.com, whose cheques with the bunny logo made for fun conversations at the bank. Jody's first article for PC Gamer was about the audio of Alien Isolation, published in 2015. Jody edited PC Gamer Indie from 2017 to 2018, and he eventually lived up to his promise to play every Warhammer videogame.

#4039. A former volunteer is threatening legal action against fan-made game project Skyblivion

A former volunteer is threatening legal action against Skyblivion, the long-running fan remake of Oblivion built in Skyrim's engine, over code they contributed to the project.

The unofficial project, which remakes 2006's The Elder Scrolls 4: Oblivion, is being made by volunteers from the TES Renewal Project, the modding group that also works on Morrowind remake Skywind.

Bethesda has allowed the project to continue on condition that it replaces all of the original game's assets, and the team continued working on it after Bethesda released its own Oblivion Remastered in April 2025.

In a statement posted to Twitter/X on 30th October, the Skyblivion team said that after the volunteer left, the two sides disagreed over the "continued use and maintenance" of their work.

A former volunteer is attempting to sue Skyblivion and we need your help pic.twitter.com/3Ee5eQTELG

The main issue was the team's decompilation of parts of that code, which it said was needed "to maintain functionality and fix issues" after its access to the original source code repository was revoked.

According to the team, the volunteer then "escalated to sending legal threats", including demands for the real names and home addresses of its volunteer team leads. The team said this was "something we couldn't accept and think is disproportionate".

The team said it has consulted legal counsel and is "completely confident in our right to maintain the code they submitted". Even so, it said it removed the code "to protect our volunteers from undue stress and ensure a clean break", rebuilding that system from scratch.

Despite this, it says the threats have continued. Its post says the former volunteer is "attempting to sue", but it's not clear whether a lawsuit has actually been filed. The volunteer has not been named.

"Please don't make this a witch-hunt," the team told fans, adding that it wishes the former volunteer "the very best" and hopes to "get this resolved as soon as possible and get on with our planned release of Skyblivion".

Last December, the team delayed Skyblivion from 2025 into 2026.

#4038. Ubisoft are reportedly tapped as one potential company that could acquire Arkane, though the Dishonored studio's own management may be in the running too

I'd really like it if it weren't Ubisoft though

Things are potentially looking up for Arkane, depending on how you feel about Ubisoft (and depending on who actually ends up acquiring them). I mention the Assassin's Creed developer because, reportedly, they're interested in buying the studio from Microsoft, having even made a bid for it. I'll go out on a limb here and say it's the whole being French thing, but uh, I'd really rather someone else bought Arkane.

This comes from, you guessed it, Bloomberg, who say that sources they've spoken with claim two other gaming companies have also made a bit. There is even the potential that Arkane would be sold to their own management, as Xbox are considering such a move. But overall, it doesn't yet sound like anything is leaning any particular way, as Xbox haven't formalised a deal with any of the potential buyers. Bloomberg also note that if a deal is made, this should then allow Arkane to finish their work on their Blade game, which is expected to release within the next couple of years.

Apparently an Xbox spokesperson told Bloomberg that the gaming company is exploring their options ahead of their December deadline, but didn't comment any further. Ubisoft reportedly did not have a comment to make on the matter. For some context on that December deadline, because of French labour laws, companies that have over 1000 staff members are required to search for a buyer for three months before they can just completely shut down. That makes December 13th the final date that such a deal has to be made by, meaning there's about a month and a half left to go.

Arkane's sale comes as part of a sweeping range of cuts, sales and closures being made by Microsoft at the moment. In July, it was announced that studios like Double Fine, Undead Labs and Compulsion would no longer be a part of Xbox, with all three going indie; Ninja Theory was also announced as part of these cuts, but unfortunately it's looking like they'll be shutting their doors. Thousands of Xbox staff were also laid off at this time, with more laid off in September, and even more coming this month and January reportedly. As always, solidarity with all workers affected by Microsoft's heartless and money hungry cuts.

Hideo Kojima is back with another review, and this time it's for Netflix spy thriller series Black Doves.

"'Black Doves' was so good that I ended up binge-watching the rest of Season 2 in one sitting," Kojima wrote on Twitter. "Season 1 was great, but Season 2 takes it to a whole new level. For fans of British spy thrillers, this is an absolute treat. The story beautifully captures the lies, love and hate, sadness, loneliness, and loyalty of spies and assassins, building up to an action-packed finale. Above all, Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw are simply outstanding. Kathryn Hunter as the handler of hired killers and Ella Lily Hyland as an assassin are also fantastic. Every single character is brilliantly written and brought to life. I could watch this forever. I really hope there’s another season. Highly recommended!"

Created by Joe Barton (The Lazarus Project), Black Doves stars Knightley as Helen, an undercover spy married to a politician named. After her lover is killed, she realizes that her cover is close to being blown... and the Black Doves send over her friend Sam (Wishaw) to protect her. In season 2, Helen is now married to the new Prime Minister... but when her handler, Mrs. Reed (Sarah Lancashire), goes missing, it's up to her and Sam to find out what the heck happened.

The first season hit Netflix in 2024, and was renewed for a second season just before its December 5 premiere date. Knightley earned a Golden Globe nomination for her performance. Black Doves season 1 holds a 92% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes (though, curiously, it has a much lower audience rating at 67%), with season 2 currently sitting at a 94% critic score based on 18 reviews.

Black Doves is streaming now on Netflix. For more, check out our guide to the best Netflix shows, and keep up with new shows on the way.

#4036. Silent Hill: Townfall adds new Hard difficulty in latest update

Silent Hill: Townfall has added a new Hard difficulty mode and rebalanced every existing setting to make room for it.

The update, patch 1.6.0, went live on PS5, Steam, and the Epic Games Store earlier this week, according to patch notes published by Konami. Konami said the rebalance is designed to create "a smoother difficulty curve for players to choose from".

As part of that rebalance, resources have been adjusted in some sections of the game, and enemies' hearing now gets sharper as the difficulty level goes up. Your position is now visible on the map in whichever mode you pick, while the reduction to the main enemy's attack severity now applies only in Story Mode.

Anyone who picks Nightmare for their first playthrough will now see a warning screen. The difficulty selection menu also gives a clearer summary of how the options differ.

SILENT HILL: TownfallNotice: Game Update (Patch 1.6.0)An update tuning gameplay and addressing some in-game issues is now available.Please check that the version number in the lower right corner of the main menu is displayed as v1.6.155963.*The PlayStation®5 version is…

The update also improves the valve status lighting for colourblind players, adds more hints and tutorials, and tweaks the wording of some puzzle hints and items. The options menu has been reorganised into clearer categories, and the controls remapping option has been renamed to make it clear that keyboard and mouse commands can be remapped there too, not just controllers.

PC players also get a new DLSS Ray Reconstruction option, alongside the usual general improvements and bug fixes.

To check you're on the latest version, look for v1.6.155963 in the lower right corner of the main menu on PC, or v1.6.156035 on PS5.

Developed by Screen Burn and published by Konami, Silent Hill: Townfall launched on PS5 and PC on 24th September. Matt said Townfall showed Silent Hill's "stellar revival continues as new developer Screen Burn melds stealth, meticulous world design, and a dash of social realism for a different sort of survival horror", and awarded it four out of five stars in Eurogamer's Silent Hill: Townfall review.

#4035. "An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process," Nexus Mods say as they rule out barring generated creations from their site

"We drew the line where the real argument is"

The owners of Nexus Mods have ruled out instituting an outright ban on AI-generated works being uploaded the site, instead opting to expand their current rules on modders disclosing how they've used AI in making their mods. This latest move to address the waves of AI-created or AI-thumbnailed mods now hitting Nexus Mods on a daily basis follows Nexus' modus operandi up to this point, which has been simply to try and ensure AI usage is clearly labelled so prospective downloaders can make informed decisions.

"We won't introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods," Nexus Mods owner and CEO Victor 'Foledinho' Folmann wrote in a news post. "You may ask me why, since that is not the solution some of you were looking for. The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process, but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.

"This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct. Mod Authors should have a chance to decide about the further use of their work, and you should be able to decide for yourselves how much AI-based content you want to see, whether more, less, or no content at all.

"As for our own position: Nexus Mods will not use your mods to train AI and will not sell or license them to anyone doing so. We refused to do that in the past, and we will refuse to do so in the future. Given such a variety of opinions within our community, not everyone will agree with any decision taken. These are the ones we believe are right for Nexus Mods today, and we’ll keep adjusting them as the tools evolve and as we see how these changes work in practice, with your feedback guiding that."

In terms of the changes which are being brought in to toughen up the site's current three tag system design to make mods containing AI-generated content, AI media, or made with AI assistance easier to spot, Nexus are making AI disclosures mandatory for those uploading new mods. "What this means is that for mods tagged as AI-assisted, we’re also introducing a requirement for a public explanation of how and where AI was used, which should give you a better understanding of what you’re downloading, rather than leaving you to make assumptions on a tag alone," Folmann wrote. "We’re also going to make AI tags on mod pages more prominent, displaying them immediately after adult-content tags so they’re easier to spot."

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that’s not going to happen," he continued. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules." New "permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods" are also being worked on, with the hopes of giving modders more control over how their works can be reused. Finally, Folmann noted that the site are "investing in security tooling and specialised staff" to address concerns over generative AI making "bespoke malicious code hidden inside mods" more prevalent.

Mod makers are being given a 60 day grace period to make sure their existing works meet the new rules, which'll run until January 2nd.

As you can imagine, the comments section of this Nexus Mods announcement is lively. Over on LinkedIn, Folmann patted himself on the back a bit about the mixed reception being an indicator the site are going about this the right way. "Some wanted a full ban. Some think we went too far. That tells me we drew the line where the real argument is," he declared, adding that "transparency beats prohibition". He also reiterated that his vision is of "modding that's Spotify-easy to play and GitHub-powerful to create, with humans in charge".

I reckon that with or without these changes, in the absence of its owners taking a strong stand browsing Nexus Mods is going to carry on be more of an exercise in ducking dodgy stuff than it was prior to most games' pages being splattered with the likes of icky AI-baked Geralt clones standing where decent screenshots of the actual game would've been more than adequate.

#4034. Guide: Cyberpunk 2077: Best Mods on PS5

What are the best Cyberpunk 2077 mods on PS5? In this guide, I'm going to highlight which mods I think are well worth installing to make your dark future experience more enticing.

On this page: Cyberpunk 2077: Best Mods on PS5

Mod support for Cyberpunk 2077 was added with Patch 2.5 on PS5, allowing for user-created content on Sony's console.

Choosing and installing mods is easy: just click the 'Mods' option on the game's main menu and you'll be taken to the current list of available mods. You can scroll through pages manually or you can use the search bar.

If you find a mod you like, select it from the list and then click the 'Install' button, or just press the Options button on your controller to install it right there and then.

You can also hit the 'Like' button to add the mod to your 'Liked' list. Doing this lets you keep track of your favourite mods via the 'Liked' filter button new the top of the screen.

You can have a maximum of 150 mods installed at any one time, and said mods need to have a combined file size of 15.76GB or under (although this isn't really an issue as of yet, as standard mod sizes tend to be very, very small).

Unfortunately, yes, using any mods disables Trophies when playing Cyberpunk 2077 on PS5.

This counts for any save file that has ever been used in conjunction with mods.

As such, you may want to beat the game at least once, or go all the way and get the Platinum, before diving into the world of mods.

Below, you'll find a list of what I think are currently the best Cyberpunk 2077 mods available on PS5.

Admittedly, the selection is far from vast at this point in time — but new mods are being added on what seems to be a weekly basis, and so this list should only grow over the coming months.

A mod that's bound to be at or near the top of Cyberpunk 2077's modding menu for years to come, Deceptious Quest Core is a necessary framework mod for a number of Deceptious' other mods.

Basically, you need to have this mod installed if you want a few of the other mods featured on this list — it's just the way that the game's quest-based modding works.

Any mod that has [DQC] in its title requires Quest Core to function.

Note that you need to enter V's H10 apartment (and then possibly exit it) for this mod to activate, and subsequently activate all of the [DQC] mods.

This mod aims to fix a surprisingly long list of bugs that are still found throughout Cyberpunk 2077.

The vast majority of these bugs are minor and only affect very small aspects of the overall game. We're talking things like slight animation glitches, specific audio mixing (those annoyingly quiet, and sometimes annoyingly loud TVs), and quest-related oddities.

Still, it's a mod worth installing when you start adding all of these fixes up — especially if you plan on starting a new playthrough.

This mod allows Johnny to appear in all of V's apartments, not just their starting home in the H10 megabuilding.

If you enjoy Johnny's company, this mod's good for immersion purposes. He'll lounge around the apartments, and add to the ambience by playing his guitar when V asks him to.

One of my favourite mods on PS5 so far, Weather Probability Rebalance does exactly what its name suggests, adjusting the chances of different weather patterns appearing as you carve out a life in Night City (and its surrounding wastelands).

For those who have already spent tens or even hundreds of hours playing Cyberpunk 2077, you may have noticed that the weather can be a bit... boring. The whole atmosphere of the city can change when it's raining, or when there's a sandstorm — but it can feel like it just doesn't happen often enough.

According to modder RMK_, the game's weather system is actually a little funky. In short, sunny weather can become 'stuck' under certain circumstances, and so this mod attempts to fix the problem.

As a result, adverse weather is much more common and lasts longer, allowing you to soak up the vibes.

A great mod for immersion purposes, Night City Interactions lets you go out drinking at various locations across the map — but the best part is that you can invite other characters, like Panam, Judy, River, and Kerry, to come along with you.

As a bonus, this mod also includes a Cyberpunk Edgerunners tour quest. As you may know, the anime features a number of backdrops that are based on actual locations from the game, and you can check these specific places out at your leisure.

Note that you need to enter V's H10 apartment (and then possibly exit) before this mod activates.

Three small mods that add just an extra touch of immersion to ripperdoc visits.

Instead of jumping straight to the cyberware menu upon talking to a ripper, V will actually sit down in the clinic's chair before undergoing surgery.

The Dogtown mod does the same for rippers in the Dogtown region of the map, while the Vic-specific mod uses Vic's existing animations from early in the game.

These are mods that, when used in conjunction with other immersion-focused mods, add up to a more detailed experience.

Another two mods that bring just a little more immersion to your time in Night City.

They let you sit down at the game's various bars and actually take a fully-animated drink. You can even select the kind of drink that you want from a dialogue menu.

What's more, the drinks give the same kind of temporary stat buffs that you get from consuming drinks in your inventory. A quick pre-gig bar crawl never hurt anyone!

Just like the Immersive Bartenders mods, this one lets you grab a fully-animated snack or drink from the numerous food vendors found across Night City.

Stat buffs are applied as if you were using items from your inventory, so it actually makes food stalls worth visiting if you're gearing up for some action.

This mod improves the readability of shards, which can be difficult to properly parse — especially if you're in a rush.

Basically, Readable Shards adjusts the text's formatting, making it slightly bigger and adding coloured names to the people who actually wrote the conversations in the first place.

This is a small mod but it can be a surprisingly big difference, particularly if you're a sucker for reading every bit of lore that you find.

A great little mod that adds a security camera system to NCARTS (metros).

By pressing left and right on the d-pad, you can switch to the cameras while you're riding the train, allowing you to view four new perspectives: two cameras shows the length of the carriage that you're on from either end, while the other two shows the outside of the metro from the front and back.

If you want to see more of Night City during your NCART travels, then this mod's an easy recommendation.

If you're absolutely sick of El Capitan giving you unreasonable time limits during his dynamic car-jacking gigs, then this mod's for you.

It simply increases said time limits by 25%, which usually equates to much easier missions. It also means that you can better enjoy the more combat-focused gigs without having to race ahead.

What are your favourite Cyberpunk 2077 mods on PS5? Hand out some recommendations in the comments section below.

I have never been particularly good at The Game of Kings, but I do love when an indie developer turns their talents to turning chess into something more funky. Shotgun King stole my heart a few years ago, and now Rulehouse is looking to offer its own spin on the classic.

Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Ted, and Rick have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager.

In a generous demo covering the first act of the game, Rulehouse presents a Wario Ware spin on things⁠—in multiple ways. Each level introduces at least one new mechanic or modifier you have to keep track of, starting with the basic "pawns only, first one to the other side of the board wins," and ramping up to a simulated prison break where guards are firing on your pieces, and you have to get your king⁠—here the game's protagonist in a prison jumpsuit⁠—to the exit.

The escalation in complexity had me genuinely scratching my head, stumped at how to proceed at a few points. Rulehouse eschews trad chess pieces as much as possible, only introducing bishops and kings by the very end of the demo⁠—and stubbornly insisting on calling knights "cows" along the way.

Instead, you get stuff like "ice pawns" that shatter on taking an opponent's piece, or "poison pawns" that bring down the opponent's piece with them when they're captured. I'm also quite fond of the upside-down pawns that move on a diagonal, and capture pieces directly in front of them.

Not every new piece is represented on each subsequent level, but it feels like Rulehouse is building a library of modifiers and complications to draw from in the final game, like how the enemy variety in a classic-style FPS campaign ramps up as you go on. It impressed me that Rulehouse could tease such novel puzzles out of one of the most studied and "solved" games to ever exist, and if it can sustain this pace of surprise and delight across a full game, I think it will prove a worthwhile puzzler.

The biggest surprise of all, though, was its presentation and sense of humor. You need something special and specific to stand out with retro pixel art these days, and Rulehouse nails the sound, look, and vibe of the Game Boy Advance. It's got the vibrant, saturated colors I associate with that special little handheld, and all the UI elements are just a little too big, like they're meant to appear on a much lower-resolution screen.

One of my favorite flourishes is how Rulehouse pairs very crisp and clean bits of pixel art with super bitcrushed and noisy backgrounds, often sourced from real photography. It's a technique that was frequently deployed on the GBA, and in addition to pure nostalgia "hey, remember this?" appeal, it adds a uniquely early aughts surreality to the proceedings, the kind I associate with stuff like Wario Ware or, less intentionally, all those really boo-boo, memory-holed movie tie-ins and ill-advised home console ports to the GBA.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

The music, similarly, nails a specific sensibility, a kind of synthy funk I associate with Wario Ware, Earthbound or, more recently, Balatro. Rulehouse is a love letter to the Game Boy Advance from people who thoroughly, obsessively, get the console.

Rulehouse is also genuinely funny. Its narrative bits have a strong rate of Smiles Per Minute™, and that dovetails nicely with the surprise rule changes and offbeat art⁠ to result in something that's just kinda nice⁠. Rulehouse is aiming to launch some time in 2027, and for now, you can wishlist it or check out the demo for yourself on Steam.
